entries.2dde79d454d5919318a52633c6edcc630dd605d4: <div sID="gen22608" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="16" osisID="Matt.16" sID="Matt.16"/> <div eID="gen22608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22609" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22610" type="x-p"/> None of Christ's miracles are recorded in this chapter, but four of his discourses. Here is, I. A conference with the Pharisees, who challenged him to show them a sign from heaven, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.1-Matt.16.4">ver. 1-4</reference>. II. Another with his disciples about the leaven of the Pharisees, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.5-Matt.16.12">ver. 5-12</reference>. III. Another with them concerning himself, as the Christ, and concerning his church built upon him, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.13-Matt.16.20">ver. 13-20</reference>. IV. Another concerning his sufferings for them, and theirs for him, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.21-Matt.16.28">ver. 21-28</reference>. And all these are written for our learning.
entries.8fdf036db98fa24e41c93e1dd05fd1b07e29f45e: <div eID="gen22610" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22609" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Sign of the Prophet Jonas.</title> <div sID="gen22611" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The Pharisees also with the Sadducees came, and tempting desired him that he would show them a sign from heaven. <hi type="super">2</hi> He answered and said unto them, When it is evening, ye say, <hi type="italic">It will be</hi> fair weather: for the sky is red. <hi type="super">3</hi> And in the morning, <hi type="italic">It will be</hi> foul weather to day: for the sky is red and lowring. O <hi type="italic">ye</hi> hypocrites, ye can discern the face of the sky; but can ye not <hi type="italic">discern</hi> the signs of the times? <hi type="super">4</hi> A wicked and adulterous generation seeketh after a sign; and there shall no sign be given unto it, but the sign of the prophet Jonas. And he left them, and departed. <div eID="gen22611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22612" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's discourse with the Pharisees and Sadducees, men at variance among themselves, as appears <reference osisRef="Acts.23.7-Acts.23.8">Acts xxiii. 7, 8</reference>, and yet unanimous in their opposition to Christ; because his doctrine did equally overthrow the errors and heresies of the Sadducees, who denied the existence of spirits and a future state; and the pride, tyranny, and hypocrisy of the Pharisees, who were the great imposters of the traditions of the elders. Christ and Christianity meet with opposition on all hands. Observe, <div eID="gen22612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22613" type="x-p"/> I. Their demand, and the design of it. <div eID="gen22613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22614" type="x-p"/> 1. The demand was of a sign from heaven; this they desired him to show them; pretending they were very willing to be satisfied and convinced, when really they were far from being so, but sought excuses from an obstinate infidelity. That which they pretended to desire was, <div eID="gen22614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22615" type="x-p"/> (1.) Some other sign than what they had yet had. They had great plenty of signs; every miracle Christ wrought was a sign, for <hi type="italic">no man could do what he did unless God were with him.</hi> But this will not serve, they must have a sign of their own choosing; they despised those signs which relieved the necessity of the sick and sorrowful, and insisted upon some sign which gratify the curiosity of the proud. It is fit that the proofs of divine revelation should be chosen by the wisdom of God, not by the follies and fancies of men. The evidence that is given is sufficient to satisfy an unprejudiced understanding, but was not intended to please a vain humour. And it is an instance of the deceitfulness of the heart, to think that we should be wrought upon by the means and advantages which we have not, while we slight those which we have. <hi type="italic">If we hear not Moses and the prophets,</hi> neither would we be wrought upon <hi type="italic">though one rose from the dead.</hi> <div eID="gen22615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22616" type="x-p"/> (2.) It must be a sign from heaven. They would have such miracles to prove his commission, as were wrought at the giving of the law upon mount Sinai: thunder, and lightening, and the voice of words, were the sign from heaven they required. Whereas the sensible signs and terrible ones were not agreeable to the spiritual and comfortable dispensation of the gospel. Now the word comes more nigh us (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.8">Rom. x. 8</reference>), and therefore the miracles do so, and do not oblige us to keep such a distance as these did, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.18">Heb. xii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen22616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22617" type="x-p"/> 2. The design was to tempt him; not to be taught by him, but to ensnare him. If he should show them a sign from heaven, they would attribute it to a confederacy with the <hi type="italic">prince of the power of the air;</hi> if he should not, as they supposed he would not, they would have that to say for themselves, <hi type="italic">why they did not believe on him.</hi> They now tempted Christ as Israel did, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.9">1 Cor. x. 9</reference>. And observe their perverseness; <hi type="italic">then,</hi> when they had signs from heaven, they tempted Christ, saying, <hi type="italic">Can he furnish a table in the wilderness?</hi> Now that he had furnished a table in the wilderness, they tempted him, saying, <hi type="italic">Can he give us a sign from heaven?</hi> <div eID="gen22617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22618" type="x-p"/> II. Christ's reply to this demand; lest they should be <hi type="italic">wise in their own conceit,</hi> he <hi type="italic">answered these fools according to their folly,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.5">Prov. xxvi. 5</reference>. In his answer, <div eID="gen22618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22619" type="x-p"/> 1. He condemns their overlooking of the signs they had, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.2-Matt.16.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. They were seeking for the signs of the kingdom of God, when it was already among them. <hi type="italic">The Lord was in this place,</hi> and they <hi type="italic">knew it not.</hi> Thus their unbelieving ancestors, when miracles were their daily bread, asked, <hi type="italic">Is the Lord among us, or is he not?</hi> <div eID="gen22619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22620" type="x-p"/> To expose this, he observes to them, <div eID="gen22620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22621" type="x-p"/> (1.) Their skilfulness and sagacity in other things, particularly in natural prognostications of the weather; "You know that a red sky over-night is a presage of fair weather, and a red sky in the morning of foul weather." There are common rules drawn from observation and experience, by which it is easy to foretel very probably what weather it will be. When second causes have begun to work, we may easily guess at their issue, so uniform is nature in its motions, and so consistent with itself. We <hi type="italic">know not the balancing of the clouds</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job xxxvii. 16</reference>), but we may spell something from the faces of them. This gives no countenance at all to the wild and ridiculous predictions of <hi type="italic">the astrologers, the star-gazers, and the monthly prognosticators</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.47.13">Isa. xlvii. 13</reference>) concerning the weather long before, with which weak and foolish people are imposed upon; we are sure, in general, that <hi type="italic">seed-time and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, shall not cease.</hi> But as to the particulars, till, by the weather-glasses, or otherwise, we perceive the immediate signs and harbingers of the change of weather, it is not for us to know, no, not <hi type="italic">that</hi> concerning the times and seasons. Let it suffice, that it shall be what weather pleases God; and that which pleases God, should not displease us. <div eID="gen22621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22622" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their sottishness and stupidity in the concerns of their souls; <hi type="italic">Can ye not discern the signs of the times?</hi> <div eID="gen22622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22623" type="x-p"/> [1.] "Do you not see that the Messiah is come?" The sceptre was departed from Judah, Daniel's weeks were just expiring, and yet they regarded not. The miracles Christ wrought, and the gathering of the people to him, were plain indications that the <hi type="italic">kingdom of heaven was at hand,</hi> that this was <hi type="italic">the day of their visitation.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There are signs of the times, by which wise and upright men are enabled to make moral prognostications, and so far to understand the motions and methods of Providence, as from thence to take their measures, and to know what Israel ought to do, as the men of Issachar, as the physician from some certain symptoms finds a crisis formed. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> There are many who are skilful enough in other things, and yet cannot or will not discern the day of their opportunities, are not aware of the wind when it is fair for them, and so let slip the gale. See <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jer. viii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa. i. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> It is great hypocrisy, when we slight the signs of God's ordaining, to seek for signs of our own prescribing. <div eID="gen22623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22624" type="x-p"/> [2.] "Do not you foresee your own ruin coming for rejecting him? You will not entertain the gospel of peace, and can you not evidently discern that hereby you pull an inevitable destruction upon your own heads?" Note, It is the undoing of multitudes, that they are not aware what will be the end of their refusing Christ. <div eID="gen22624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22625" type="x-p"/> 2. He refuses to give them any other sign (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.4">v. 4</reference>), as he had done before in the same words, <reference osisRef="Matt.12.39">ch. xii. 39</reference>. Those that persist in the same iniquities, must expect to meet with the same reproofs. Here, as there, (1.) He calls them <hi type="italic">an adulterous generation;</hi> because, while they professed themselves of the true church and spouse of God, they treacherously departed from him, and brake their covenants with him. The Pharisees were <hi type="italic">a generation pure in their own eyes,</hi> having the way of the adulterous woman, that thinks she has done no wickedness, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.20">Prov. xxx. 20</reference>. (2.) He refuses to gratify their desire. Christ will not be prescribed to; <hi type="italic">we ask, and have not, because we ask amiss.</hi> (3.) He refers them to the sign of the prophet Jonas, which should yet be given them; his resurrection from the dead, and his preaching by his apostles to the Gentiles; these were reserved for the last and highest evidences of his divine mission. Note, Though the fancies of proud men shall not be humoured, yet the faith of the humble shall be supported, and the unbelief of them that perish left for ever inexcusable, and <hi type="italic">every mouth shall be stopped.</hi> <div eID="gen22625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22626" type="x-p"/> This discourse broke off abruptly; <hi type="italic">he left them and departed.</hi> Christ will not tarry long with those that tempt him, but justly withdraws from those that are disposed to quarrel with him. He left them as irreclaimable; <hi type="italic">Let them alone.</hi> He left them to themselves, left them in the hand of their own counsels; <hi type="italic">so he gave them up to their own hearts' lust.</hi>
entries.8685cb4a94ed336d3b9d01af47a8bea6fa7b888e: <div eID="gen22626" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Of the Leaven of the Pharisees.</title> <div sID="gen22627" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> And when his disciples were come to the other side, they had forgotten to take bread. <hi type="super">6</hi> Then Jesus said unto them, Take heed and beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees. <hi type="super">7</hi> And they reasoned among themselves, saying, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> because we have taken no bread. 8 <hi type="italic">Which</hi> when Jesus perceived, he said unto them, O ye of little faith, why reason ye among yourselves, because ye have brought no bread? <hi type="super">9</hi> Do ye not yet understand, neither remember the five loaves of the five thousand, and how many baskets ye took up? <hi type="super">10</hi> Neither the seven loaves of the four thousand, and how many baskets ye took up? <hi type="super">11</hi> How is it that ye do not understand that I spake <hi type="italic">it</hi> not to you concerning bread, that ye should beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees? <hi type="super">12</hi> Then understood they how that he bade <hi type="italic">them</hi> not beware of the leaven of bread, but of the doctrine of the Pharisees and of the Sadducees. <div eID="gen22627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22628" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's discourse with his disciples concerning bread, in which, as in many other discourses, he speaks to them of spiritual things under a similitude, and they misunderstand him of carnal things. The occasion of it was, their forgetting to victual their ship, and to take along with them provisions for their family on the other side of the water; usually they carried bread along with them, because they were sometimes in desert places; and when they were not, yet they would not be burthensome. But now they forgot; we will hope it was because their minds and memories were filled with better things. Note, Christ's disciples are often such as have no great forecast for the world. <div eID="gen22628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22629" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the caution Christ gave them, to <hi type="italic">beware of the leaven of the Pharisees.</hi> He had now been discoursing with the Pharisees and Sadducees, and saw them to be men of such a spirit, that it was necessary to caution his disciples to have nothing to do with them. Disciples are in most danger from hypocrites; against those that are openly vicious they stand upon their guard, but against Pharisees, who are great pretenders to devotion, and Sadducees, who pretend to a free and impartial search after truth, they commonly lie unguarded: and therefore the caution is doubted, <hi type="italic">Take heed, and beware.</hi> <div eID="gen22629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22630" type="x-p"/> The corrupt principles and practices of the Pharisees and Sadducees are compared to leaven; they were souring, and swelling, and spreading, like leaven; they fermented wherever they came. <div eID="gen22630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22631" type="x-p"/> II. Their mistake concerning this caution, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.7">v. 7</reference>. They thought Christ hereby upbraided them with their improvidence and forgetfulness, that they were so busy attending to his discourse with the Pharisees, that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they forgot their private concerns. Or, because having no bread of their own with them, they must be beholden to their friends for supply, he would not have them to ask it of the Pharisees and Sadducees, nor to receive of <hi type="italic">their</hi> alms, because he would not so far countenance them; or, for fear, lest, under pretence of feeding them, they should do them a mischief. Or, they took it for a caution, not to be familiar with the Pharisees and Sadducees, not to eat with them (<reference osisRef="Prov.23.6">Prov. xxiii. 6</reference>), whereas the danger was not in their bread (Christ himself did eat with them, <reference osisRef="Luke.7.36">Luke vii. 36</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.11.37">xi. 37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.14.1">xiv. 1</reference>), but in their principles. <div eID="gen22631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22632" type="x-p"/> III. The reproof Christ gave them for this. <div eID="gen22632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22633" type="x-p"/> 1. He reproves their distrust of his ability and readiness to supply them in this strait (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.8">v. 8</reference>); "<hi type="italic">O ye of little faith,</hi> why are ye in such perplexity because ye have <hi type="italic">taken no bread,</hi> that ye can mind nothing else, that ye think your Master is as full of it as you, and apply every thing he saith to that?" He does not chide them for their little forecast, as they expected he would. Note, Parents and masters must not be angry at the forgetfulness of their children and servants, more than is necessary to make them take more heed another time; we are all apt to be forgetful of our duty. This should serve to excuse a fault, <hi type="italic">Peradventure it was an oversight.</hi> See how easily Christ forgave his disciples' carelessness, though it was in such a material point as taking bread; and do likewise. But that which he chides them for is their little faith. <div eID="gen22633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22634" type="x-p"/> (1.) He would have them to depend upon him for supply, though it were in a wilderness, and not to disquiet themselves with anxious thoughts about it. Note, Though Christ's disciples be brought into wants and straits, through their own carelessness and incogitancy, yet he encourages them to trust in him for relief. We must not therefore use this as an excuse for our want of charity to those who are really poor, that they should have minded their own affairs better, and then they would not have been in need. It may be so, but they must not therefore be left to starve when they are in need. <div eID="gen22634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22635" type="x-p"/> (2.) He is displeased at their solicitude in this matter. The weakness and shiftlessness of good people in their worldly affairs is that for which men are apt to condemn them; but it is not such an offence to Christ as their inordinate care and anxiety about those things. We must endeavour to keep the mean between the extremes of carelessness and carefulness; but of the two, the excess of thoughtfulness about the world worst becomes Christ's disciples. "<hi type="italic">O ye of little faith,</hi> why are ye disquieted for want of bread?" Note, To distrust Christ, and to disturb ourselves when we are in straits and difficulties, is an evidence of the weakness of our faith, which, if it were in exercise as it should be, would ease us of the burthen of care, by casting it on the Lord, who <hi type="italic">careth for us.</hi> <div eID="gen22635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22636" type="x-p"/> (3.) The aggravation of their distrust was the experience they had so lately had of the power and goodness of Christ in providing for them, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.9-Matt.16.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Though they had no bread with them, they had him with them who could provide bread for them. If they had not the cistern, they had the Fountain. <hi type="italic">Do ye not yet understand, neither remember?</hi> Note, Christ's disciples are often to be blamed for the shallowness of their understandings, and the slipperiness of their memories. "Have ye forgot those repeated instances of merciful and miraculous supplies; five thousand fed with five loaves, and four thousand with seven loaves, and yet they had enough and to spare? Remember <hi type="italic">how many baskets ye took up.</hi>" These baskets were intended for memorials, by which to keep the mercy in remembrance, as the pot of manna which was preserved in the ark, <reference osisRef="Exod.16.32">Exod. xvi. 32</reference>. The fragments of those meals would be a feast now; and he that could furnish them with such an overplus then, surely could furnish them with what was necessary now. That meat for their bodies was intended to be meat or their faith (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.14">Ps. lxxiv. 14</reference>), which therefore they should have lived upon, now that they had forgotten to take bread. Note, We are <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> perplexed with present cares and distrusts, because we do not duly remember our former experiences of divine power and goodness. <div eID="gen22636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22637" type="x-p"/> 2. He reproves their misunderstanding of the caution he gave them (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.11">v. 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">How is it that you do not understand?</hi> Note, Christ's disciples may well be ashamed of the slowness and dulness of their apprehensions in divine things; especially when they have long enjoyed the means of grace; <hi type="italic">I spake it not unto you concerning bread.</hi> He took it ill, (1.) That they should think him as thoughtful about bread as they were; whereas his <hi type="italic">meat and drink were to do his Father's will.</hi> (2.) That they should be so little acquainted with his way of preaching, as to take that literally which he spoke by way of parable; and should thus make themselves like the multitude, who, when Christ spoke to them in parables, seeing, saw not, and hearing, heard not, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.13">ch. xiii. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen22637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22638" type="x-p"/> IV. The rectifying of the mistake by this reproof (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.12">v. 12</reference>); <hi type="italic">Then understood they</hi> what he meant. Note, Christ <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> shows us our folly and weakness, that we may stir up ourselves to take things right. He did not tell them expressly what he meant, but repeated what he had said, that they should beware of the leaven; and so obliged them, by comparing this with his other discourses, to arrive at the sense of it in their own thoughts. Thus Christ teaches by the Spirit of wisdom in the heart, opening the understanding to the Spirit of revelation in the word. And those truths are most precious, which we have thus digged for, and have found out after some mistakes. Though Christ did not tell them plainly, yet now they were aware that by the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, he meant their doctrine and way, which were corrupt and vicious, but, as they managed them, very apt to insinuate themselves into the minds of men like leaven, and to <hi type="italic">eat like a canker.</hi> They were leading men, and were had in reputation, which made the danger of infection by their errors the greater. In our age, we may reckon atheism and deism to be the leaven of the Sadducees, and popery to be the leaven of the Pharisees, against both which it concerns all Christians to stand upon their guard.
entries.2fb8646be5f0da9eb6ae58198e17e4338760f406: <div eID="gen22638" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ's Conference with His Disciples.</title> <div sID="gen22639" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> When Jesus came into the coasts of Cæsarea Philippi, he asked his disciples, saying, Whom do men say that I the Son of man am? <hi type="super">14</hi> And they said, Some <hi type="italic">say that thou art</hi> John the Baptist: some, Elias; and others, Jeremias, or one of the prophets. <hi type="super">15</hi> He saith unto them, But whom say ye that I am? <hi type="super">16</hi> And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-jona: for flesh and blood hath not revealed <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto thee, but my Father which is in heaven. <hi type="super">18</hi> And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. <hi type="super">19</hi> And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven. <hi type="super">20</hi> Then charged he his disciples that they should tell no man that he was Jesus the Christ. <div eID="gen22639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22640" type="x-p"/> We have here a private conference which Christ had with his disciples concerning himself. It was in the coasts of Cesarea Philippi, the utmost borders of the land of Canaan northward; there in that remote corner, perhaps, there was less flocking after him than in other places, which gave him leisure for this private conversation with his disciples. Note, When ministers are abridged in their public work, they should endeavour to do the more in their own families. <div eID="gen22640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22641" type="x-p"/> Christ is here catechising his disciples. <div eID="gen22641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22642" type="x-p"/> I. He enquires what the opinions of others were concerning him; <hi type="italic">Who do men say that I, the Son of man, am?</hi> <div eID="gen22642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22643" type="x-p"/> 1. He calls himself the <hi type="italic">Son of man;</hi> which may be taken either, (1.) As a title common to him with others. He was called, and justly, <hi type="italic">the Son of God,</hi> for so he was (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.35">Luke i. 35</reference>); but he called himself the Son of man; for he is really and truly "Man, made of a woman." In courts of honour, it is a rule to distinguish men by their highest titles; but Christ, having now emptied himself, though he was the Son of God, will be known by the style and title of the Son of man. Ezekiel was often so called to <hi type="italic">keep</hi> him humble; Christ called himself so, to show that he <hi type="italic">was</hi> humble. Or, (2.) As a title peculiar to him as Mediator. He is made known, in Daniel's vision, as the <hi type="italic">Son of man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.7.13">Dan. vii. 13</reference>. I am the Messiah, that Son of man that was promised. But, <div eID="gen22643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22644" type="x-p"/> 2. He enquires what people's sentiments were concerning him: "<hi type="italic">Who do men say that I am? The Son of man?</hi>" (So I think it might better be read). "Do they own me for the Messiah?" He asks not, "Who do the <hi type="italic">scribes</hi> and <hi type="italic">Pharisees</hi> say that I am?" They were prejudiced against him, and said that he was a deceiver and in league with Satan; but, "Who do <hi type="italic">men</hi> say that I am?" He referred to the common people, whom the Pharisees despised. Christ asked this question, not as one that knew not; for if he knows what men think, much more what they say; nor as one desirous to hear his own praises, but to make the disciples solicitous concerning the success of their preaching, by showing that he himself was so. The common people conversed more familiarly with the disciples than they did with their Master, and therefore from them he might better know what they said. Christ had not plainly said who he was, but left people to infer it from his works, <reference osisRef="John.10.24-John.10.25">John x. 24, 25</reference>. Now he would know what inferences the people drew from <hi type="italic">them,</hi> and from the miracles which his apostles wrought in his name. <div eID="gen22644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22645" type="x-p"/> 3. To this question the disciples have him an answer (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.14">v. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">Some say, thou art John the Baptist, &c.</hi> There were some that said, he was the <hi type="italic">Son of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.23">ch. xii. 23</reference>), and the great Prophet, <reference osisRef="John.6.14">John vi. 14</reference>. The disciples, however, do not mention that opinion, but only such opinions as were wide of the truth, which they gathered up from their countrymen. Observe, <div eID="gen22645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22646" type="x-p"/> (1.) They are different opinions; some say one thing, and others another. Truth is one; but those who vary from that commonly vary one from another. Thus Christ came eventually to send division, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.51">Luke xii. 51</reference>. Being so noted a Person, every one would be ready to pass his verdict upon him, and, "Many men, many minds;" those that were not willing to own him to be the Christ, wandered in endless mazes, and followed the chase of every uncertain guess and wild hypothesis. <div eID="gen22646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22647" type="x-p"/> (2.) They are honourable opinions, and bespeak the respect they had for him, according to the best of their judgment. These were not the sentiments of his enemies, but the sober thoughts of those that followed him with love and wonder. Note, It is possible for men to have good thoughts of Christ, and yet not right ones, a high opinion of him, and yet not high enough. <div eID="gen22647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22648" type="x-p"/> (3.) They all suppose him to be <hi type="italic">one risen from the dead;</hi> which perhaps arose from a confused notion they had of the resurrection of the Messiah, before his public preaching, as of Jonas. Or their notions arose from an excessive value for antiquity; as if it were not possible for an excellent man to be produced in their own age, but it must be one of the ancients returned to life again. <div eID="gen22648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22649" type="x-p"/> (4.) They are all false opinions, built upon mistakes, and wilful mistakes. Christ's doctrines and miracles bespoke him to be an extraordinary Person; but because of the meanness of his appearance, so different from what they expected, they would not own him to be the Messiah, but will grant him to be any thing rather than that. <div eID="gen22649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22650" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">Some say, thou art John the Baptist.</hi> Herod said so (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.2">ch. xiv. 2</reference>), and those about him would be apt to say as he said. This notion might be strengthened by an opinion they had, that those who died as martyrs, should rise again before others; which some think the second of the seven sons refers to, in his answer to Antiochus, <reference osisRef="2Macc.7.9">2 Macc. vii. 9</reference>, <hi type="italic">The King of the world shall raise us up, who have died for his laws, unto everlasting life.</hi> <div eID="gen22650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22651" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">Some Elias;</hi> taking occasion, no doubt, from the prophecy of Malachi (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.5">ch. iv. 5</reference>), <hi type="italic">Behold, I will send you Elijah.</hi> And the rather, because Elijah (as Christ) did many miracles, and was himself, in his translation, the greatest miracle of all. <div eID="gen22651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22652" type="x-p"/> [3.] <hi type="italic">Others Jeremias:</hi> they fasten upon him, either because he was the weeping prophet, and Christ was often in tears; or because God had <hi type="italic">set him over the kingdoms and nations</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.1.10">Jer. i. 10</reference>), which they thought agreed with their notion of the Messiah. <div eID="gen22652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22653" type="x-p"/> [4.] <hi type="italic">Or, one of the prophets.</hi> This shows what an honourable idea they entertained of the prophets; and yet they were <hi type="italic">the children of them that persecuted and slew them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.23.29">ch. xxiii. 29</reference>. Rather than they would allow Jesus of Nazareth, one of their own country, to be such an extraordinary Person as his works bespoke him to be, they would say, "It was not he, but <hi type="italic">one of the old prophets.</hi>" <div eID="gen22653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22654" type="x-p"/> II. He enquires what <hi type="italic">their</hi> thoughts were concerning him; "<hi type="italic">But who say ye that I am?</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.16.15">v. 15</reference>. Ye tell me what other people say of me; can ye say better?" 1. The disciples had themselves been better taught than others; had, by their intimacy with Christ, greater advantages of getting knowledge than others had. Note, It is justly expected that those who enjoy greater plenty of the means of knowledge and grace than others, should have a more clear and distinct knowledge of the things of God than others. Those who have more acquaintance with Christ than others, should have truer sentiments concerning him, and be able to give a better account of him than others. 2. The disciples were trained up to teach others, and therefore it was highly requisite that they should understand the truth themselves: "Ye that are to preach the gospel of the kingdom, what are your notions of him that sent you?" Note, Ministers must be examined before they be sent forth, especially what their sentiments are of Christ, and who they say that he is; for how can they be owned as ministers of Christ, that are either ignorant or erroneous concerning Christ? This is a question we should every one of us be frequently putting to ourselves, "<hi type="italic">Who</hi> do we say, <hi type="italic">what</hi> kind of one do we say, that <hi type="italic">the Lord Jesus is?</hi> Is he precious to us? Is he in our eyes the chief of ten thousand? Is he the Beloved of our souls?" It is well or ill with us, according as our thoughts are right or wrong concerning Jesus Christ. <div eID="gen22654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22655" type="x-p"/> Well, this is the question; now let us observe, <div eID="gen22655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22656" type="x-p"/> (1.) Peter's answer to this question, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.16">v. 16</reference>. To the former question concerning the opinion others had of Christ, several of the disciples answered, according as they had heard people talk; but to this Peter answers in the name of all the rest, they all consenting to it, and concurring in it. Peter's temper led him to be forward in speaking upon all such occasions, and sometimes he spoke well, sometimes amiss; in all companies there are found some warm, bold men, to whom a precedency of speech falls of course; Peter was such a one: yet we find other of the apostles sometimes speaking as the mouth of the rest; as <hi type="italic">John</hi> (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.38">Mark ix. 38</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thomas, Philip,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jude,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.14.5">John xiv. 5</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.8">8</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.14.22">22</reference>. So that this is far from being a proof of such primacy and superiority of Peter above the rest of the apostles, as the church of Rome ascribes to him. They will needs advance him to be a judge, when the utmost they can make of him, is, that he was but foreman of the jury, to speak for the rest, and that only <hi type="italic">pro h&#226;c vice—for this once;</hi> not the perpetual dictator or speaker of the house, only chairman upon this occasion. <div eID="gen22656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22657" type="x-p"/> Peter's answer is short, but it is full, and true, and to the purpose; <hi type="italic">Thou art the Christ, the Son of the Living God.</hi> Here is a confession of the Christian faith, addressed to Christ, and so made an act of devotion. Here is a confession of the true God as the living God, in opposition to dumb and dead idols, and of <hi type="italic">Jesus Christ, whom he hath sent,</hi> whom to know is <hi type="italic">life eternal.</hi> This is the conclusion of the whole matter. <div eID="gen22657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22658" type="x-p"/> [1.] The people called him <hi type="italic">a Prophet, that Prophet</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.6.14">John vi. 14</reference>); but the disciples own him to be the Christ, the anointed One; the great Prophet, Priest, and King of the church; the true Messiah promised to the fathers, and depended on by them as <hi type="italic">He that shall come.</hi> It was a great thing to believe this concerning one whose outward appearance was so contrary to the general idea the Jews had of the Messiah. <div eID="gen22658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22659" type="x-p"/> [2.] He called himself the <hi type="italic">Son of Man;</hi> but they owned him to be <hi type="italic">the Son of the living God.</hi> The <hi type="italic">people's</hi> notion of him was, that he was the ghost of a dead man, Elias, or Jeremias; but <hi type="italic">they</hi> know and believe him to be <hi type="italic">the Son of the living God,</hi> who has life in himself, and has given to his Son to have life in himself, and to be the <hi type="italic">Life of the world.</hi> If he be <hi type="italic">the Son of the living God,</hi> he is of the same nature with him: and though his divine nature was now veiled with the cloud of flesh, yet there were those who looked through it, and <hi type="italic">saw his glory, the glory as of the Only-Begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.</hi> Now can we with an assurance of faith subscribe to this confession? Let us then, with a fervency of affection and adoration, go to Christ, and tell him so; Lord Jesus, <hi type="italic">thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God.</hi> <div eID="gen22659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22660" type="x-p"/> (2.) Christ's approbation of his answer (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.17-Matt.16.19">v. 17-19</reference>); in which Peter is replied to, both as a believer and as an apostle. <div eID="gen22660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22661" type="x-p"/> [1.] As a believer, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.17">v. 17</reference>. Christ shows himself well pleased with Peter's confession, that it was so clear and express, without <hi type="italic">ifs</hi> or <hi type="italic">ands,</hi> as we say. Note, The proficiency of Christ's disciples in knowledge and grace is very acceptable to him; and Christ shows him whence he received the knowledge of this truth. At the first discovery of this truth in the dawning of the gospel day, it was a mighty thing to believe it; <hi type="italic">all men had not this knowledge,</hi> had not this faith. But, <div eID="gen22661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22662" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Peter had the happiness of it; <hi type="italic">Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-jona.</hi> He reminds him of his rise and original, the meanness of his parentage, the obscurity of his extraction; he was <hi type="italic">Bar-jonas—The son of a dove;</hi> so some. Let him remember <hi type="italic">the rock out of which he was hewn,</hi> that he may see he was not born to this dignity, but preferred to it by the divine favour; it was free grace that made him to differ. Those that have received the Spirit must remember who is their Father, <reference osisRef="1Sam.10.12">1 Sam. x. 12</reference>. Having reminded him of this, he makes him sensible of his great happiness as a believer; <hi type="italic">Blessed art thou.</hi> Note, True believers are truly blessed, and those are blessed indeed whom Christ pronounces blessed; his saying they are so, makes them so. "Peter, thou art a happy man, who thus <hi type="italic">knowest the joyful sound,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.89.15">Ps. lxxxix. 15</reference>. <hi type="italic">Blessed are your eyes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.13.16">ch. xiii. 16</reference>. All happiness attends the right knowledge of Christ. <div eID="gen22662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22663" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> God must have the glory of it; "<hi type="italic">For flesh and blood have not revealed it to thee.</hi> Thou hadst this neither by the invention of thy own wit and reason, nor by the instruction and information of others; this light sprang neither from nature nor from education, but from my Father who is in heaven." Note, 1. The Christian religion is a revealed religion, has its rise in heaven; it is a religion from above, given by inspiration of God, not the learning of philosophers, nor the politics of statesmen. 2. Saving faith is the gift of God, and, wherever it is, is wrought by him, as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, for his sake, and upon the score of his mediation, <reference osisRef="Phil.1.29">Phil. i. 29</reference>. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> thou art blessed, because <hi type="italic">my Father has revealed it to thee.</hi> Note, The revealing of Christ to us and in us is a distinguishing token of God's good will, and a firm foundation of true happiness; and blessed are they that are thus highly favoured. <div eID="gen22663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22664" type="x-p"/> Perhaps Christ discerned something of pride and vain-glory in Peter's confession; a subtle sin, and which is apt to mingle itself even with our good duties. It is hard for good men to compare themselves with others, and not to have too great a conceit of themselves; to prevent which, we should consider that our preference to others is no achievement of our own, but the free gift of God's grace too us, and not to others; so that we have nothing to boast of, <reference osisRef="Ps.115.1">Ps. cxv. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.7">1 Cor. iv. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen22664" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22665" type="x-p"/> [2.] Christ replies to him as an apostle or minister, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.18-Matt.16.19">v. 18, 19</reference>. Peter, in the name of the church, had confessed Christ, and to him therefore the promise intended for the church is directed. Note, There is nothing lost by being forward to confess Christ; for those who honour him, he will honour. <div eID="gen22665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22666" type="x-p"/> Upon occasion of this great confession made of Christ, which is the church's homage and allegiance, he signed and published this royal, this divine charter, by which that body politic is incorporated. Such is the communion between Christ and the church, the Bridegroom and the spouse. God had a church in the world from the beginning, and it was built upon the rock of the promised Seed, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.15">Gen. iii. 15</reference>. But now, that promised Seed being come, it was requisite that the church should have a new charter, as Christian, and standing in relation to a Christ already come. Now here we have that charter; and a thousand pities it is, that this word, which is the great support of the kingdom of Christ, should be wrested and pressed into the service of antichrist. But the devil has employed his subtlety to pervert it, as he did that promise, <reference osisRef="Ps.91.11">Ps. xci. 11</reference>, which he perverted to his own purpose, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.6">ch. iv. 6</reference>, and perhaps both that scripture and this he thus perverted because they stood in his way, and therefore he owed them a spite. <div eID="gen22666" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22667" type="x-p"/> Now the purport of this charter is, <div eID="gen22667" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22668" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To establish the being of the church; <hi type="italic">I say also unto thee.</hi> It is Christ that makes the grant, he who is the church's Head, and Ruler, to whom all judgment is committed, and from whom all power is derived; he who makes it pursuant to the authority received from the Father, and his undertaking for the salvation of the elect. The grant is put into Peter's hand; "I say it to <hi type="italic">thee.</hi>" The Old Testament promises relating to the church were given immediately to particular persons, eminent for faith and holiness, as to Abraham and David; which yet gave no supremacy to them, much less to any of their successors; so the New-Testament charter is here delivered to Peter as an agent, but to the use and behoof of the church in all ages, according to the purposes therein specified and contained. Now it is here promised, <div eID="gen22668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22669" type="x-p"/> 1. That Christ would build his church upon a rock. This body politic is incorporated by the style and title of <hi type="italic">Christ's church.</hi> It is a number o the children of men called out of the world, and set apart from it, and dedicated to Christ. It is not <hi type="italic">thy</hi> church, but <hi type="italic">mine.</hi> Peter remembered this, when he cautioned ministers <hi type="italic">not to lord it over God's heritage.</hi> The church is Christ's peculiar, appropriated to him. The world is God's, and they that dwell therein; but the church is a chosen remnant, that stands in relation to God through Christ as Mediator. It bears him image and superscription. <div eID="gen22669" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22670" type="x-p"/> (1.) The Builder and Maker of the church is Christ himself; <hi type="italic">I will build it.</hi> The church is a temple which Christ is the Builder of, <reference osisRef="Zech.6.11-Zech.6.13">Zech. vi. 11-13</reference>. Herein Solomon was a type of Christ, and Cyrus, <reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">Isa. xliv. 28</reference>. The materials and workmanship are his. By the working of his Spirit with the preaching of his word he adds souls to his church, and so builds it up with living stones, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1 Pet. ii. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Ye are God's building;</hi> and building is a progressive work; the church in this world is but <hi type="italic">in fieri—in the forming,</hi> like a house in the building. It is a comfort to all those who wish well to the church, that Christ, who has divine wisdom and power, undertakes to build it. <div eID="gen22670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22671" type="x-p"/> (2.) The foundation on which it is built is, <hi type="italic">this Rock.</hi> Let the architect do his part ever so well, if the foundation be rotten, the building will not stand; let us therefore see what the foundation is, and it must be meant of Christ, for <hi type="italic">other foundation can no man lay.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa. xxviii. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen22671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22672" type="x-p"/> [1.] The church is built upon a <hi type="italic">rock;</hi> a firm, strong, and lasting foundation, which time will not waste, nor will it sink under the weight of the building. Christ would not build his house upon the sand, for he knew that storms would arise. A rock is high, <reference osisRef="Ps.61.2">Ps. lxi. 2</reference>. Christ's church does not stand upon a level with this world; a rock is large, and extends far, so does the church's foundation; and the more large, the more firm; those are not the church's friends that narrow its foundation. <div eID="gen22672" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22673" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is built upon <hi type="italic">this</hi> rock; thou art <hi type="italic">Peter,</hi> which signifies <hi type="italic">a stone or rock;</hi> Christ gave him that name when he first called him (<reference osisRef="John.1.42">John i. 42</reference>), and here he confirms it; "Peter, thou dost answer thy name, thou art a solid, substantial disciple, fixed and stayed, and one that there is some hold of. Peter is thy name, and strength and stability are with thee. Thou art not shaken with the waves of men's fluctuating opinions concerning me, but established in the present truth," <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.12">2 Pet. i. 12</reference>. From the mention of this significant name, occasion is taken for this metaphor of <hi type="italic">building upon a rock.</hi> <div eID="gen22673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22674" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Some by this rock understand Peter himself as an apostle, the chief, though not the prince, of the twelve, senior among them, but not superior over them. The church is built upon the foundation of the apostles, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Eph. ii. 20</reference>. The first stones of that building were laid in and by their ministry; hence their names are said to be <hi type="italic">written in the foundations</hi> of the new Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Rev.21.14">Rev. xxi. 14</reference>. Now Peter being that apostle by whose hand the first stones of the church were laid, both in Jewish converts (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1-Acts.2.47">Acts ii.</reference>), and in the Gentile converts (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.1-Acts.10.48">Acts x.</reference>), he might in some sense be said to be the rock on which it was built. <hi type="italic">Cephas</hi> was one that seemed to be a pillar, <reference osisRef="Gal.2.9">Gal. ii. 9</reference>. But it sounds very harsh, to call a man that only lays the first stone of a building, which is a transient act, the foundation on which it is built, which is an abiding thing. Yet if it were so, this would not serve to support the pretensions of the Bishop of Rome; for Peter had no such headship as he claims, much less could he derive it to his successors, least of all to the Bishops of Rome, who, whether they are so in place or no, is a question, but that they are not so in the truth of Christianity, is past all question. <div eID="gen22674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22675" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Others, by this <hi type="italic">rock,</hi> understand <hi type="italic">Christ; "Thou art Peter,</hi> thou hast the name of a <hi type="italic">stone,</hi> but <hi type="italic">upon this rock,</hi> pointing to himself, <hi type="italic">I will build my church.</hi>" Perhaps he laid his hand on his breast, as when he said, <hi type="italic">Destroy this temple</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.2.19">John ii. 19</reference>), when he <hi type="italic">spoke of the temple of his body.</hi> Then he took occasion from the temple, where he was, so to speak of himself, and gave occasion to some to misunderstand him of that; so here he took occasion from Peter, to speak of himself as the Rock, and gave occasion to some to misunderstand him of Peter. But this must be explained by those many scriptures which speak of Christ as the only Foundation of the church; see <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">1 Cor. iii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.6">1 Pet. ii. 6</reference>. Christ is both its Founder and its Foundation; he draws souls, and draws them to himself; to him they are united, and on him they rest and have a constant dependence. <div eID="gen22675" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22676" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Others by this <hi type="italic">rock</hi> understand this confession which Peter made of Christ, and this comes all to one with understanding it of Christ himself. It was a good confession which Peter witnessed, <hi type="italic">Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God;</hi> the rest concurred with him in it. "Now," saith Christ, "this is that great truth <hi type="italic">upon which I will build my church.</hi>" 1. Take away this truth itself, and the universal church falls to the ground. If Christ be not the Son of God, Christianity is a cheat, and the church is a mere chimera; <hi type="italic">our preaching is vain, your faith is vain, and you are yet in your sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.14-1Cor.15.17">1 Cor. xv. 14-17</reference>. If Jesus be not the Christ, those that own him are not of the church, but deceivers and deceived. 2. Take away the faith and confession of this truth from any particular church, and it ceases to be a part of Christ's church, and relapses to the state and character of infidelity. This is <hi type="italic">articulus stantis et cadentis ecclesia—that article, with the admission or the denial of which the church either rises or falls;</hi> "the main hinge on which the door of salvation turns;" those who let go this, do not hold the foundation; and though they may call themselves Christians, they give themselves the lie; for the church is a sacred society, incorporated upon the certainty and assurance of this great truth; and great it is, and has prevailed. <div eID="gen22676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22677" type="x-p"/> 2. Christ here promises to preserve and secure his church, when it is built; <hi type="italic">The gates of hell shall not prevail against it;</hi> neither against this truth, nor against the church which is built upon it. <div eID="gen22677" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22678" type="x-p"/> (1.) This implies that the church has enemies that fight against it, and endeavour its ruin overthrow, here represented by <hi type="italic">the gates of hell, that is,</hi> the city of hell; (which is directly opposite to this heavenly city, this <hi type="italic">city of the living God</hi>), the devil's interest among the children of men. The gates of hell are the powers and policies of the devil's kingdom, the dragon's head and horns, by which he <hi type="italic">makes war with the Lamb;</hi> all that comes out of hell-gates, as being hatched and contrived there. These fight against the church by opposing gospel truths, corrupting gospel ordinances, persecuting good ministers and good Christians; drawing or driving, persuading by craft or forcing by cruelty, to that which is inconsistent with the purity of religion; this is the design of the gates of hell, to root out the name of Christianity (<reference osisRef="Ps.83.4">Ps. lxxxiii. 4</reference>), <hi type="italic">to devour the man-child</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.9">Rev. xii. 9</reference>), to raze this city to the ground. <div eID="gen22678" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22679" type="x-p"/> (2.) This assures us that the enemies of the church shall not gain their point. While the world stands, Christ will have a church in it, in which his truths and ordinances shall be owned and kept up, in spite of all the opposition of the powers of darkness; <hi type="italic">They shall not prevail against it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.129.1-Ps.129.2">Ps. cxxix. 1, 2</reference>. This gives no security to any particular church, or church-governors that they shall never err, never apostatize or be destroyed; but that somewhere or other the Christian religion shall have a being, though not always in the same degree of purity and splendour, yet so as that the entail of it shall never be quite cut off. The <hi type="italic">woman lives, though in a wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.12.14">Rev. xii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">cast down but not destroyed</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.4.9">2 Cor. iv. 9</reference>). Corruptions grieving, persecutions grievous, but neither fatal. The church may be foiled in particular encounters, but in the main battle it shall come off <hi type="italic">more than a conqueror.</hi> Particular believers are <hi type="italic">kept by the power of God, through faith, unto salvation,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.5">1 Pet. i. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen22679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22680" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The other part of this charter is, to settle the order and government of the church, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.19">v. 19</reference>. When a city or society is incorporated, officers are appointed and empowered to act for the common good. A city without government is a chaos. Now this constituting of the government of the church, is here expressed by the delivering of the keys, and, with them, a power to bind and loose. This is not to be understood of any peculiar power that Peter was invested with, as if he were sole door-keeper of the kingdom of heaven, and had that key of David which belongs only to the Son of David; no, this invests all the apostles and their successors with a ministerial power to guide and govern the church of Christ, as it exists in particular congregations or churches, according to the rules of the gospel. <hi type="italic">Claves regni cælorum in B. Petro apostolo cuncti suscepimus sacerdotes—All we that are priests, received, in the person of the blessed apostle Peter, the keys of the kingdom of heaven;</hi> so Ambrose <hi type="italic">De Dignit. Sacerd.</hi> Only the keys were first put into Peter's hand, because he was the first <hi type="italic">that opened the door of faith to the Gentiles,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.10.28">Acts x. 28</reference>. As the king, in giving a charter to a corporation, empowers the magistrates to hold courts in his name, to try matters of fact, and determine therein according to law, confirming what is so done regularly as if done in any of the superior courts; so Christ, having incorporated his church, hath appointed the office of the ministry for the keeping up of order and government, and to see that his laws be duly served; <hi type="italic">I will give thee the keys.</hi> He doth not say, "I <hi type="italic">have</hi> given them," or "I <hi type="italic">do</hi> now;" but "I <hi type="italic">will</hi> do it," meaning after his resurrection; <hi type="italic">when he ascended on high, he gave those gifts,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Ephes. iv. 8</reference>; then this power was actually given, not to Peter only, but to all the rest, <reference osisRef="Matt.28.19-Matt.28.20">ch. xxviii. 19, 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.21">John xx. 21</reference>. He doth not say, The keys <hi type="italic">shall</hi> be given, but, <hi type="italic">I will give</hi> them; for ministers derive their authority from Christ, and all their power is to be used in his name, <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.4">1 Cor. v. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen22680" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22681" type="x-p"/> Now, 1. The power here delegated is a spiritual power; it is a power <hi type="italic">pertaining to the kingdom of heaven,</hi> that is, to the church, that part of it which is militant here on earth, to the gospel dispensation; that is it about which the apostolical and ministerial power is wholly conversant. It is not any civil, secular power that is hereby conveyed, Christ's <hi type="italic">kingdom is not of this world;</hi> their instructions afterward were <hi type="italic">in things pertaining to the kingdom of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.1.3">Acts i. 3</reference>. <div eID="gen22681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22682" type="x-p"/> 2. It is the <hi type="italic">power</hi> of the keys that is given, alluding to the custom of investing men with authority in such a place, by delivering to them the keys of the place. Or as the master of the house gives the keys to the steward, the keys of the stores where the provisions are kept, that he may give to every one in the house <hi type="italic">his portion of meat in due season</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.42">Luke xii. 42</reference>), and deny it as there is occasion, according to the rules of the family. Ministers are <hi type="italic">stewards,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.4.1">1 Cor. iv. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.7">Tit. i. 7</reference>. Eliakim, who had <hi type="italic">the key</hi> of the house of David, <hi type="italic">was over the household,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.22.22">Isa. xxii. 22</reference>. <div eID="gen22682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22683" type="x-p"/> 3. It is a power to <hi type="italic">bind and loose,</hi> that is (following the metaphor of the keys), to shut and open. Joseph, who was lord of Pharaoh's house, and steward of the stores, had power <hi type="italic">to bind his princes, and to teach his senators wisdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.105.21-Ps.105.22">Ps. cv. 21, 22</reference>. When the stores and treasures of the house are shut up from any, they are bound, <hi type="italic">interdico tibi aqu&#226; et igne—I forbid thee the use of fire and water;</hi> when they are opened to them again, they are loosed from that bond, are discharged from the censure, and restored to their liberty. <div eID="gen22683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22684" type="x-p"/> 4. It is a power which Christ has promised to own the due administration of; he will ratify the sentences of his stewards with his own approbation; <hi type="italic">It shall be bound in heaven, and loosed in heaven:</hi> not that Christ hath hereby obliged himself to confirm all church-censures, right or wrong; but such as are duly passed according to the word, <hi type="italic">clave non errante—the key turning the right way,</hi> such are sealed in heaven; that is, the word of the gospel, in the mouth of faithful ministers, is to be looked upon, not as the word of man, but as the word of God, and to be received accordingly, <reference osisRef="1Thess.2.13">1 Thess. ii. 13</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.12.20">John xii. 20</reference>. <div eID="gen22684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22685" type="x-p"/> Now <hi type="italic">the keys of the kingdom of heaven are,</hi> <div eID="gen22685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22686" type="x-p"/> (1.) The key of <hi type="italic">doctrine,</hi> called the key of <hi type="italic">knowledge.</hi> "Your business shall be to explain to the world the will of God, both as to truth and duty; and for this you shall have your commissions, credentials, and full instructions to bind and loose:" these, in the common speech of the Jews, at that time, signified to prohibit and permit; to teach or declare a thing to be unlawful was to <hi type="italic">bind;</hi> to be lawful, was to <hi type="italic">loose.</hi> Now the apostles had an extraordinary power of this kind; some things forbidden by the law of Moses were now to be allowed, as the eating of such and such meats; some things allowed there were now to be forbidden, as divorce; and the apostles were empowered to declare this to the world, and men might take it upon their words. When Peter was first taught himself, and then taught others, <hi type="italic">to call nothing common or unclean,</hi> this power was exercised. There is also an ordinary power hereby conveyed to all ministers, to preach the gospel as appointed officers; to tell people, in God's name, and according to the scriptures, <hi type="italic">what is good, and what the Lord requires of them:</hi> and they who <hi type="italic">declare the whole counsel of God,</hi> use these keys well, <reference osisRef="Acts.20.27">Acts xx. 27</reference>. <div eID="gen22686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22687" type="x-p"/> Some make the giving of the keys to allude to the custom of the Jews in creating a doctor of the law, which was to put into his hand the keys of the chest where the book of the law was kept, denoting his being authorized to take and read it; and <hi type="italic">the binding and loosing,</hi> to allude to the fashion about their books, which were in rolls; they shut them by binding them up with a string, which they untied when they opened them. Christ gives his apostles power to shut or open the book of the gospel to people, as the case required. See the exercise of this power, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.46">Acts xiii. 46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.6">xviii. 6</reference>. When ministers preach pardon and peace to the penitent, wrath and the curse to the impenitent, in Christ's name, they act then pursuant to this authority of binding and loosing. <div eID="gen22687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22688" type="x-p"/> (2.) The key of <hi type="italic">discipline,</hi> which is but the application of the former to particular persons, upon a right estimate of their characters and actions. It is not legislative power that is hereby conferred, but judicial; the judge doth not make the law, but only declares what is law, and upon an impartial enquiry into the merits of the cause, gives sentence accordingly. Such is <hi type="italic">the power of the keys,</hi> wherever it is lodged, with reference to church-membership and the privileges thereof. [1.] Christ's ministers have a power to admit into the church; "<hi type="italic">Go, disciple all nations, baptizing them;</hi> those who profess faith in Christ, and obedience to him, admit them and their seed members of the church by baptism." Ministers are to let in to <hi type="italic">the wedding-feast those that are bidden;</hi> and to keep out such as are apparently unfit for so holy a communion. [2.] They have a power to expel and cast out such as have forfeited their church-membership, that is binding; refusing to unbelievers the application of gospel promises and the seals of them; and declaring to such as appear to be <hi type="italic">in the gall of bitterness and bond of iniquity,</hi> that <hi type="italic">they have no part or lot in the matter,</hi> as Peter did to Simon Magus, though he had been baptized; and this is a binding over to the judgment of God. [3.] They have a power to restore and to receive in again, upon their repentance, such as had been thrown out; to loose those whom they had bound; declaring to them, that, if their repentance be sincere, the promise of pardon belongs to them. The apostles had a miraculous gift of <hi type="italic">discerning spirits;</hi> yet even <hi type="italic">they</hi> went by the rule of outward appearances (as <reference osisRef="Acts.8.21">Acts viii. 21</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.1-1Cor.5.2">1 Cor. v. 1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.7">2 Cor. ii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.20">1 Tim. i. 20</reference>), which ministers may still make a judgment upon, if they be skilful and faithful. <div eID="gen22688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22689" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Here is the charge which Christ gave his disciples, to keep this private for the present (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.20">v. 20</reference>); <hi type="italic">They must tell no man that he was Jesus the Christ.</hi> What they had professed to him, they must not yet publish to the world, for several reasons; 1. Because this was the time of preparation for his kingdom: the great thing now preached, was, that <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven was at hand;</hi> and therefore those things were now to be insisted on, which were proper to make way for Christ; as the doctrine of repentance; not this great truth, in and with which <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven</hi> was to be actually set up. Every thing is beautiful in its season, and it is good advice, <hi type="italic">Prepare thy work, and afterwards build,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.24.27">Prov. xxiv. 27</reference>. 2. Christ would have his Messiahship proved by his works, and would rather <hi type="italic">they</hi> should testify of him than that his <hi type="italic">disciples</hi> should, because their testimony was but as his own, which he insisted not on. See <reference osisRef="John.5.31">John v. 31</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.5.34">34</reference>. He was so secure of the demonstration of his miracles, that he waived other witnesses, <reference osisRef="John.10.25">John x. 25</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.10.38">38</reference>. 3. If they had known <hi type="italic">that he was Jesus the Christ, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1 Cor. ii. 8</reference>. 4. Christ would not have the apostles preach this, till they had the most convincing evidence ready to allege in confirmation of it. Great truths may suffer damage by being asserted before they can be sufficiently proved. Now the great proof of Jesus being the Christ was his resurrection: by that <hi type="italic">he was declared to be the Son of God, with power;</hi> and therefore the divine wisdom would not have this truth preached, till that could be alleged for proof of it. 5. It was requisite that the preachers of so great a truth should be furnished with greater measures of the Spirit than the apostles as yet had; therefore the open asserting of it was adjourned till the Spirit should be poured out upon them. But when Christ was glorified and the Spirit poured out, we find Peter proclaiming upon the house-tops what was here spoken in a corner (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.36">Acts ii. 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">That God hath made this same Jesus both Lord and Christ;</hi> for, as there is a time to keep silence, so there is a time to speak.
entries.7a9d50a421b2b051e13d5a379702be8c2cc2a974: <div eID="gen22689" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ Reproves Peter.</title> <div sID="gen22690" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">21</hi> From that time forth began Jesus to show unto his disciples, how that he must go unto Jerusalem, and suffer many things of the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and be raised again the third day. <hi type="super">22</hi> Then Peter took him, and began to rebuke him, saying, Be it far from thee, Lord: this shall not be unto thee. <hi type="super">23</hi> But he turned, and said unto Peter, Get thee behind me, Satan: thou art an offence unto me: for thou savourest not the things that be of God, but those that be of men. <div eID="gen22690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22691" type="x-p"/> We have here Christ's discourse with his disciples concerning his own sufferings; in which observe, <div eID="gen22691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22692" type="x-p"/> I. Christ's foretelling of his sufferings. Now he <hi type="italic">began</hi> to do it, and from this time he frequently spake of them. Some hints he had already given of his sufferings, as when he said, <hi type="italic">Destroy this temple:</hi> when he spake of <hi type="italic">the Son of man being lifted up,</hi> and of <hi type="italic">eating his flesh, and drinking his blood:</hi> but now he <hi type="italic">began</hi> to show it, to speak plainly and expressly of it. Hitherto he had not touched upon this, because the disciples were weak, and could not well bear the notice of a thing so very strange, and so very melancholy; but now that they were more ripe in knowledge, and strong in faith, he began to tell them this. Note, Christ reveals his mind to his people gradually, and lets in light as they can bear it, and are fit to receive it. <div eID="gen22692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22693" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">From that time,</hi> when they had made that full confession of Christ, that he was the Son of God, then he began to show them this. When he found them knowing in one truth, he taught them another; <hi type="italic">for to him that has, shall be given.</hi> Let them first be established in the principles of the doctrine of Christ, and then go on to perfection, <reference osisRef="Heb.6.1">Heb. vi. 1</reference>. If they had not been well grounded in the belief of Christ's being the Son of God, it would have been a great shaking to their faith. All truths are not to be spoken to all persons at all times, but such as are proper and suitable to their present state. Now observe, <div eID="gen22693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22694" type="x-p"/> 1. What he foretold concerning his sufferings, the particulars and circumstances of them, and all surprising. <div eID="gen22694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22695" type="x-p"/> (1.) The place where he should suffer. He must go to Jerusalem, the head city, the holy city, and suffer there. Though he lived most of his time in Galilee, he must die at Jerusalem; there all the sacrifices were offered, there therefore <hi type="italic">he</hi> must die, <hi type="italic">who is the great sacrifice.</hi> <div eID="gen22695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22696" type="x-p"/> (2.) The persons by whom he should suffer; <hi type="italic">the elders, and chief priests, and scribes;</hi> these made up the great sanhedrim, which sat at Jerusalem, and was had in veneration by the people. Those that should have been most forward in owning and admiring Christ, were the most bitter in persecuting him. It was strange that men of knowledge in the scripture, who professed to expect the Messiah's coming, and pretended to have something sacred in their character, should use him thus barbarously when he did come. It was the Roman power that condemned and crucified Christ, but he lays it at the door of <hi type="italic">the chief priests and scribes,</hi> who were the first movers. <div eID="gen22696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22697" type="x-p"/> (3.) What he should suffer; <hi type="italic">he must suffer many things, and be killed.</hi> His enemies' insatiable malice, and his own invincible patience, appear in the variety and multiplicity of his sufferings (he suffered many things) and in the extremity of them; nothing less than his death would satisfy them, he must be killed. The suffering of many things, if not unto death, is more tolerable; for while there is life, there is hope; and death, without such prefaces, would be less terrible; but <hi type="italic">he must</hi> first <hi type="italic">suffer many things, and then be killed.</hi> <div eID="gen22697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22698" type="x-p"/> (4.) What should be the happy issue of all his sufferings; he shall <hi type="italic">be raised again the third day.</hi> As the prophets, so Christ himself, when he testified beforehand his sufferings, testified withal the glory that should follow, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>. His rising again the third day proved him to be the Son of God, notwithstanding his sufferings; and therefore he mentions that, to keep up their faith. When he spoke of the cross and the shame, he spoke in the same breath of <hi type="italic">the joy set before him,</hi> in the prospect of which <hi type="italic">he endured the cross, and despised the shame.</hi> Thus we must look upon Christ's suffering for us, trace in it the way to his glory; and thus we must look upon our suffering for Christ, look through it to the recompence of reward. <hi type="italic">If we suffer with him, we shall reign with him.</hi> <div eID="gen22698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22699" type="x-p"/> 2. Why he foretold his sufferings. (1.) To show that they were the product of an eternal counsel and consent; were agreed upon between the Father and the Son from eternity; <hi type="italic">Thus is behoved Christ to suffer.</hi> The matter was settled in <hi type="italic">the determinate counsel and foreknowledge,</hi> in pursuance of his own voluntary susception and undertaking for our salvation; his sufferings were no surprise to him, did not come upon him as a snare, but he had a distinct and certain foresight of them, which greatly magnifies his love, <reference osisRef="John.18.4">John xviii. 4</reference>. (2.) To rectify the mistakes which his disciples had imbibed concerning the external pomp and power of his kingdom. Believing him to be the Messiah, they counted upon nothing but dignity and authority in the world; but here Christ reads them another lesson, tells them of the cross and sufferings; nay, that the chief priests and the elders, whom, it is likely, they expected to be the supports of the Messiah's kingdom, should be its great enemies and persecutors; this would give them quite another idea of that kingdom which they themselves had preached the approach of; and it was requisite that this mistake should be rectified. Those that follow Christ must be dealt plainly with, and warned not to expect great things in this world. (3.) It was to prepare them for the share, at least, of sorrow and fear, which they must have in his sufferings. When he suffered many things, the disciples could not but suffer some; if their Master be killed, they will be seized with terror; let them know it before, that they may provide accordingly, and, being fore-<hi type="italic">warned,</hi> may be fore-<hi type="italic">armed.</hi> <div eID="gen22699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22700" type="x-p"/> II. The offence which Peter took at this he said, <hi type="italic">Be it far from thee, Lord:</hi> probably he spake the sense of the rest of the disciples, as before, for he was chief speaker. <hi type="italic">He took him, and began to rebuke him.</hi> Perhaps Peter was a little elevated with the great things Christ had how said unto him, which made him more bold with Christ than did become him; so hard is it to keep the spirit low and humble in the midst of great advancements! <div eID="gen22700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22701" type="x-p"/> 1. It did not become Peter to contradict his Master, or take upon him to advise him; he might have wished, <hi type="italic">that, if it were possible, this cup might pass away,</hi> without saying so peremptorily, <hi type="italic">This shall not be,</hi> when Christ had said, <hi type="italic">It must be. Shall any teach God knowledge? He that reproveth God, let him answer it.</hi> Note, When God's dispensations are either intricate or cross to us, it becomes us silently to acquiesce in, and not to prescribe to, the divine will; God knows what he has to do, without our teaching. Unless we know the mind of the Lord, it is not for us to be his counsellors, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">Rom. xi. 34</reference>. <div eID="gen22701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22702" type="x-p"/> 2. It savoured much of fleshly wisdom, for him to appear so warmly against suffering, and to startle thus at the offence of the cross. It is the corrupt part of us, that is thus solicitous to sleep in a whole skin. We are apt to look upon sufferings as they relate to this present life, to which they are uneasy; but there are other rules to measure them by, which, if duly observed, will enable us cheerfully to bear them, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.18">Rom. viii. 18</reference>. See how passionately Peter speaks: "<hi type="italic">Be it far from thee, Lord.</hi> God forbid, that thou shouldst suffer and be killed; we cannot bear the thoughts of it." <hi type="italic">Master, spare thyself:</hi> so it might be read; <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">hileos soi, kyrie</hi></hi>—"<hi type="italic">Be merciful to thyself,</hi> and then no one else can be cruel to thee; pity thyself, and then <hi type="italic">this shall not be to thee.</hi>" He would have Christ to dread suffering as much as he did; but we mistake, if we measure Christ's love and patience by our own. He intimates, likewise, the improbability of the thing, humanly speaking; "<hi type="italic">This shall not be unto thee.</hi> It is impossible that one who hath so great an interest in the people as thou hast, should be crushed by the elders, who fear the people: this can never be; we that have followed thee, will fight for thee, if occasion be; and there are thousands that will stand by us." <div eID="gen22702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22703" type="x-p"/> III. Christ's displeasure against Peter for this suggestion of his, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.23">v. 23</reference>. We do not read of any thing said or done by any of his disciples, at any time, that he resented so much as this, though they often offended. <div eID="gen22703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22704" type="x-p"/> Observe, 1. How he expressed his displeasure: He turned upon Peter, and (we may suppose) with a frown said, <hi type="italic">Get thee behind me, Satan.</hi> He did not so much as take time to deliberate upon it, but gave an immediate reply to the temptation, which was such as made it to appear how ill he took it. Just now, he had said, <hi type="italic">Blessed art thou, Simon,</hi> and had even laid him in his bosom; but here, <hi type="italic">Get thee behind me, Satan;</hi> and there was cause for both. Note, A good man may by a surprise of temptation soon grow very unlike himself. He answered him as he did Satan himself, <reference osisRef="Matt.4.10">ch. iv. 10</reference>. Note, (1.) It is the subtlety of Satan, to send temptations to us by the unsuspected hands of our best and dearest friends. Thus he assaulted Adam by Eve, Job by his wife, and here Christ by his beloved Peter.
