It concerns us therefore not to be ignorant of his devices, but to stand against his wiles and depths, by standing always upon our guard against sin, whoever moves us to it. Even the kindnesses of our friends are often abused by Satan, and made use of as temptations to us. (2.) Those who have their spiritual senses exercised, will be aware of the voice of Satan, even in a friend, a disciple, a minister, that dissuades them from their duty. We must not regard who speaks, so much as what is spoken; we should learn to know the devil's voice when he speaks in a saint as well as when he speaks in a serpent. Whoever takes us off from that which is good, and would have us afraid of doing too much for God, speaks Satan's language. (3.) We must be free and faithful in reproving the dearest friend we have, that saith or doth amiss, though it may be under colour of kindness to us. We must not compliment, but rebuke, mistaken courtesies. <hi type="italic">Faithful are the wounds of a friend.</hi> Such smitings must be accounted kindnesses, <reference osisRef="Ps.141.5">Ps. cxli. 5</reference>. (4.) Whatever appears to be a temptation to sin, must be resisted with abhorrence, and not parleyed with. <div eID="gen22704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22705" type="x-p"/> 2. What was the ground of this displeasure; why did Christ thus resent a motion that seemed not only harmless, but kind? Two reasons are given: <div eID="gen22705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22706" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Thou art an offence to me</hi>—<hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">Skandalon mou ei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">Thou art my hindrance</hi> (so it may be read); "thou standest in my way." Christ was hastening on in the work of our salvation, and his heart was so much upon it, that he took it ill to be hindered, or tempted to start back from the hardest and most discouraging part of his undertaking. So strongly was he engaged for our redemption, that they who but indirectly endeavoured to divert him from it, touched him in a very tender and sensible part. Peter was not so sharply reproved for disowning and denying his Master in his sufferings as he was for dissuading him from them; though that was the defect, this the excess, of kindness. It argues a very great firmness and resolution of mind in any business, when it is <hi type="italic">an offence</hi> to be dissuaded, and a man will not endure to hear any thing to the contrary; like that of Ruth, <hi type="italic">Entreat me not to leave thee.</hi> Note, Our Lord Jesus preferred our salvation before his own ease and safety; for <hi type="italic">even Christ pleased not himself</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rom.15.3">Rom. xv. 3</reference>); he came into the world, not to spare himself, as Peter advised, but to spend himself. <div eID="gen22706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22707" type="x-p"/> See why he called Peter <hi type="italic">Satan,</hi> when he suggested this to him; because, whatever stood in the way of our salvation, he looked upon as coming from the devil, who is a sworn enemy to it. The same Satan that afterward entered into Judas, maliciously to destroy him in his undertaking, here prompted Peter plausibly to divert him from it. Thus <hi type="italic">he changes himself into an angel of light.</hi> <div eID="gen22707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22708" type="x-p"/> Thou art an offence to me. Note, [1.] Those that engage in any great good work must expect to meet with hindrance and opposition from friends and foes, from within and from without. [2.] Those that obstruct our progress in any duty must be looked upon as an offence to us. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> we do the will of God as Christ did, <hi type="italic">whose meat and drink it was to do it,</hi> when it is a trouble to us to be solicited from our duty. Those that hinder us from doing or suffering for God, when we are called to it, whatever they are in other things in that they are <hi type="italic">Satans, adversaries</hi> to us. <div eID="gen22708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22709" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Thou savourest not the things that are of God, but those that are of men.</hi> Note, [1.] <hi type="italic">The things that are of God,</hi> that is, the concerns of his will and glory, often clash and interfere with <hi type="italic">the things that are of men,</hi> that is, with our own wealth, pleasure, and reputation. While we mind Christian duty as our way and work, and the divine favour as our end and portion, we <hi type="italic">savour the things of God;</hi> but if these be minded, the flesh must be denied, hazards must be run and hardships borne; and here is the trial which of the two we savour. [2.] Those that inordinately fear, and industriously decline suffering for Christ, when they are called to it, savour more of the things of man than of the things of God; they relish those things more themselves, and make it appear to others that they do so.
entries.a8b46e70bf96b600c1c62f10171325418a3bb185: <div eID="gen22709" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Value of the Soul.</title> <div sID="gen22710" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Then said Jesus unto his disciples, If any <hi type="italic">man</hi> will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. <hi type="super">25</hi> For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. <hi type="super">26</hi> For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? <hi type="super">27</hi> For the Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works. <hi type="super">28</hi> Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom. <div eID="gen22710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22711" type="x-p"/> Christ, having shown his disciples that <hi type="italic">he</hi> must suffer, and that he was ready and willing to suffer, here shows them that <hi type="italic">they</hi> must suffer too, and must be ready and willing. It is a weighty discourse that we have in these verses. <div eID="gen22711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22712" type="x-p"/> I. Here is the law of discipleship laid down, and the terms fixed, upon which we may have the honour and benefit of it, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.24">v. 24</reference>. He said this to his disciples, not only that they might instruct others concerning it, but that by this rule they might examine their own security. Observe, <div eID="gen22712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22713" type="x-p"/> 1. What it is to be a disciple of Christ; it is to come after him. When Christ called his disciples, this was the word of command, <hi type="italic">Follow me.</hi> A true disciple of Christ is one that doth follow him in duty, and shall follow him to glory. He is one that comes after Christ, not one that prescribes to him, as Peter now undertook to do, forgetting his place. A disciple of Christ comes after him, as the sheep after the shepherd, the servant after his master, the soldiers after their captain; he is one that aims at the same end that Christ aimed at, the glory of God, and the glory of heaven: and one that walks in the same way that he walked in, is led by his Spirit, treads in his steps, submits to his conduct, and <hi type="italic">follows the Lamb, whithersoever he goes,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 4</reference>. <div eID="gen22713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22714" type="x-p"/> 2. What are the great things required of those that will be Christ's disciples; <hi type="italic">If any man will come,</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ei tis thelei</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">If any man be willing</hi> to come. It denotes a deliberate choice, and cheerfulness and resolution in that choice. Many are disciples more by chance or the will of others than by any act of their own will; but Christ will have his people volunteers, <reference osisRef="Ps.110.3">Ps. cx. 3</reference>. It is as if Christ had said, "If any of the people that are not my disciples, be steadfastly minded to come to me, and if you that are, be in like manner minded to adhere to me, it is upon these terms, these and no other; you must <hi type="italic">follow me</hi> in sufferings as well as in other things, and therefore when you sit down to count the cost, reckon upon it." <div eID="gen22714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22715" type="x-p"/> Now what are these terms? <div eID="gen22715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22716" type="x-p"/> (1.) <hi type="italic">Let him deny himself.</hi> Peter had advised Christ to spare himself, and would be ready, in the like case, to take the advice; but Christ tells them all, they must be so far from <hi type="italic">sparing</hi> themselves, that they must <hi type="italic">deny</hi> themselves. Herein they must come after Christ, for his birth, and life, and death, were all a continued act of self-denial, a self-emptying, <reference osisRef="Phil.2.7-Phil.2.8">Phil. ii. 7, 8</reference>. If self-denial be a hard lesson, and against the grain to flesh and blood, it is no more than what our Master learned and practised before us and for us, both for our redemption and for our instruction; and <hi type="italic">the servant is not above his lord.</hi> Note, All the disciples and followers of Jesus Christ must deny themselves. It is the fundamental law of admission into Christ's school, and the first and great lesson to be learned in this school, to deny ourselves; it is both the <hi type="italic">strait</hi> gate, and the <hi type="italic">narrow</hi> way; it is necessary in order to our learning all the other good lessons that are there taught. We must deny ourselves absolutely, we must not admire our own shadow, nor gratify our own humour; we must not lean to our own understanding, nor seek our own things, nor be our own end. We must deny ourselves comparatively; we must deny ourselves for Christ, and his will and glory, and the service of his interest in the world; we must deny ourselves for our brethren, and for their good; and we must deny ourselves for ourselves, deny the appetites of the body for the benefit of the soul. <div eID="gen22716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22717" type="x-p"/> (2.) <hi type="italic">Let him take up his cross.</hi> The cross is here put for all sufferings, as men or Christians; providential afflictions, persecutions for righteousness' sake, every trouble that befals us, either for doing well or for not doing ill. The troubles of Christians are fitly called <hi type="italic">crosses,</hi> in allusion to the death of the cross, which Christ was obedient to; and it should reconcile us to troubles, and take off the terror of them, that they are what we bear in common with Christ, and such as he hath borne before us. Note, [1.] Every disciple of Christ hath his cross, and must count upon it; as each hath his special duty to be done, so each hath his special trouble to be borne, and every one feels most from his own burthen. Crosses are the common lot of God's children, but of this common lot each hath his particular share. That is our cross which Infinite Wisdom has appointed for us, and a Sovereign Providence has laid on us, as fittest for us. It is good for us to call the cross we are under <hi type="italic">our own,</hi> and entertain it accordingly. We are apt to think we could bear such a one's cross better than our own; but that is best which is, and we ought to make the best of it. [2.] Every disciple of Christ must take up that which the wise God hath made his cross. It is an allusion to the Roman custom of compelling those that were condemned to be crucified, to carry their cross: when Simon carried Christ's cross after him, this phrase was illustrated. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It is supposed that the cross lies in our way, and is prepared for us. We must not make crosses to ourselves, but must accommodate ourselves to those which God has made for us. Our rule is, not to go a step out of the way of duty, either to meet a cross, or to miss one. We must not by our rashness and indiscretion pull crosses down upon our own heads, but must take them up when they are laid in our way. We must so manage an affliction, that it may not be a stumbling-block or hindrance to us in any service we have to do for God. We must take it up out of our way, by getting over <hi type="italic">the offence of the cross; None of these things move me;</hi> and we must then go on with it in our way, though it lie heavy. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> That which we have to do, is, not only to bear the cross (that a stock, or a stone, or a stick may do), not only to be silent under it, but we must <hi type="italic">take up</hi> the cross, must improve it to some good advantage. We should not say, "This is an evil, and I must bear it, because I cannot help it;" but, "This is an evil, and I will bear it, because it shall work for my good." When we <hi type="italic">rejoice in our afflictions, and glory in them,</hi> then we take up the cross. This fitly follows upon denying ourselves; for he that will not deny himself the pleasures of sin, and the advantages of this world for Christ, when it comes to the push, will never have the heart to take up his cross. "He that cannot take up the resolution to live a saint, has a demonstration within himself, that he is never likely to die a martyr;" so Archbishop Tillotson. <div eID="gen22717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22718" type="x-p"/> (3.) <hi type="italic">Let him follow me,</hi> in this particular of taking up the cross. Suffering saints must look unto Jesus, and take from him both direction and encouragement in suffering. Do we bear the cross? We therein follow Christ, who bears it <hi type="italic">before</hi> us, bears it <hi type="italic">for</hi> us, and so bears it <hi type="italic">from</hi> us. He bore the heavy end of the cross, the end that had the curse upon it, that was a heavy end, and so made the other light and easy for us. Or, we may take it in general, we must follow Christ in all instances of holiness and obedience. Note, The disciples of Christ must study to imitate their Master, and conform themselves in every thing to his example, and continue in well-doing, whatever crosses lie in their way. To do well and to suffer ill, is to follow Christ. <hi type="italic">If any man will come after me, let him follow me;</hi> that seems to be <hi type="italic">idem per idem—the same thing over again.</hi> What is the difference? Surely it is this, "<hi type="italic">If any man will come after me,</hi> in profession, and so have the name and credit of a disciple, <hi type="italic">let him follow me in truth,</hi> and so do the work and duty of a disciple." Or thus, "<hi type="italic">If any man will set out after me,</hi> in good beginnings, <hi type="italic">let him</hi> continue to <hi type="italic">follow me</hi> with all perseverance." That is <hi type="italic">following the Lord fully,</hi> as Caleb did. Those that come after Christ, must follow after him. <div eID="gen22718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22719" type="x-p"/> II. Here are arguments to persuade us to submit to these laws, and come up to these terms. Self-denial, and patient suffering, are hard lessons, which will never be learned if we consult with flesh and blood; let us therefore consult with our Lord Jesus, and see what advice he gives us; and here he gives us, <div eID="gen22719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22720" type="x-p"/> 1. Some considerations proper to engage us to these duties of self-denial and suffering for Christ. Consider, <div eID="gen22720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22721" type="x-p"/> (1.) The weight of that eternity which depends upon our present choice (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.25">v. 25</reference>); <hi type="italic">Whosoever will save his life,</hi> by denying Christ, <hi type="italic">shall lose it: and whosoever</hi> is content to <hi type="italic">lose his life,</hi> for owning Christ, <hi type="italic">shall find it.</hi> Here are <hi type="italic">life and death, good and evil, the blessing and the curse, set before us.</hi> Observe, <div eID="gen22721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22722" type="x-p"/> [1.] The misery that attends the most plausible apostasy. <hi type="italic">Whosoever will save his life</hi> in this world, if it be by sin, he <hi type="italic">shall lose it</hi> in another; he that forsakes Christ, to preserve a temporal life and avoid a temporal death, will certainly come short of eternal life, and will be hurt of the second death, and eternally held by it. There cannot be a fairer pretence for apostasy and iniquity than saving the life by it, so cogent is the law of self-preservation; and yet even that is folly, for it will prove in the end self-destruction; the life saved is but for a moment, the death shunned is but as a sleep; but the life lost is everlasting, and the death run upon is the depth and complement of all misery, and an endless separation from all good. Now, let any rational man consider of it, take advice and speak his mind, whether there is any thing got, at long run, by apostasy, though a man save his estate, preferment, or life, by it. <div eID="gen22722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22723" type="x-p"/> [2.] The advantage that attends the most perilous and expensive constancy; <hi type="italic">Whosoever will lose his life for Christ's sake</hi> in this world, <hi type="italic">shall find it</hi> in a better, infinitely to his advantage. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Many a life is lost, for Christ's sake, in doing his work, by labouring fervently for his name; in suffering work, by choosing rather to die than to deny him or his truths and ways. Christ's holy religion is handed down to us, sealed with the blood of thousands, that have <hi type="italic">not known their own souls,</hi> but have <hi type="italic">despised their lives</hi> (as Job speaks in another case), though very valuable ones, when they have stood in competition with their duty and <hi type="italic">the testimony of Jesus,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.20.4">Rev. xx. 4</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Though many have been losers for Christ, even of life itself, yet never any one was, or will be, a loser by him in the end. The loss of other comforts, for Christ, may possibly be made up in this world (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.30">Mark x. 30</reference>); the loss of life cannot, but it shall be made up in the other world, in an eternal life; the believing prospect of which hath been the great support of suffering saints in all ages. An assurance of the life they should find, in lieu of the life they hazarded, hath enabled them to triumph over death in all its terrors; to go smiling to a scaffold, and stand singing at a stake, and to call the utmost instances of their enemies' rage but <hi type="italic">a light affliction.</hi> <div eID="gen22723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22724" type="x-p"/> [3.] The worth of the soul which lies at stake, and the worthlessness of the world in comparison of it (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">v. 26</reference>). <hi type="italic">What is a man profited, if he gain the whole world and lose his own soul?</hi> <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">ten psychen autou</hi></hi>; the same word which is translated <hi type="italic">his life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.25">v. 25</reference>), for the <hi type="italic">soul</hi> is the <hi type="italic">life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen. ii. 7</reference>. This alludes to that common principle, that, whatever a man gets, if he lose his life, it will do him no good, he cannot enjoy his gains. But it looks higher, and speaks of the soul as immortal, and a loss of it beyond death, which cannot be compensated by the gain of the whole world. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Every man has a soul of his own. The soul is the spiritual and immortal part of man, which thinks and reasons, has a power of reflection and prospect, which actuates the body now, and will shortly act in a separation from the body. Our souls are our own not in respect of dominion and property (for we are not our <hi type="italic">own, All souls are mine,</hi> saith God), but in respect of nearness and concern; our souls are our own, for they are ourselves. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It is possible for the soul to be lost, and there is danger of it. The soul is lost when it is eternally separated from all the good to all the evil that a soul is capable of; when it dies as far as a soul can die; when it is separated from the favour of God, and sunk under his wrath and curse. A man is never undone till he is in hell. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> If the soul be lost, it is of the sinner's own losing. The <hi type="italic">man loses his own soul,</hi> for he does that which is certainly destroying to it, and neglects that which alone would be saving, <reference osisRef="Hos.13.9">Hos. xiii. 9</reference>. The sinner dies because he will die; <hi type="italic">his blood is on his own head. Fourthly,</hi> One soul is worth more than all the world; our own souls are of greater value to us than all the wealth, honour, and pleasures of this present time, if we had them. Here is <hi type="italic">the whole world</hi> set in the scale against <hi type="italic">one soul,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Tekel</hi> written upon it; it is weighed in the balance, and found too light to weigh it down. This is Christ's judgment upon the matter, and he is a competent Judge; he had reason to know the price of <hi type="italic">souls,</hi> for he redeemed them; nor would he under-rate the world, for he made it. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> The winning of the world is often the losing of the soul. Many a one has ruined his eternal interest by his preposterous and inordinate care to secure and advance his temporal ones. It is <hi type="italic">the love of the world,</hi> and the eager pursuit of it, <hi type="italic">that drowns men in destruction and perdition. Sixthly,</hi> The loss of the soul is so great a loss, that the gain of the whole world will not countervail it, or make it up. He that loses his soul, though it be to gain the world, makes a very bad bargain for himself, and will sit down at last an unspeakable loser. When he comes to balance the account, and to compare profit and loss, he will find that, instead of the advantage he promised himself, he is ruined to all intents and purposes, is irreparably broken. <div eID="gen22724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22725" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">What shall a man give in exchange for his soul?</hi> Note, If once the soul be lost, it is lost for ever. There is no <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">antallagma</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">counter-price,</hi> that can be paid, or will be accepted. It is a loss that can never be repaired, never be retrieved. If, after that great price which Christ laid down to redeem our souls, and to restore us to the possession of them, they be so neglected for the world, that they come to be lost, that new mortgage will never be taken off; there remains no more sacrifice for sins, nor price for souls, but the equity of redemption is eternally precluded. Therefore it is good to be wise in time, and do well for ourselves. <div eID="gen22725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22726" type="x-p"/> 2. Here are some considerations proper to encourage us in self-denial and suffering for Christ. <div eID="gen22726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22727" type="x-p"/> (1.) The assurance we have of Christ's glory, at his second coming to judge the world, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.27">v. 27</reference>. If we look to the end of all these things, the period of the world, and the posture of souls then, we shall thence form a very different idea of the present state of things. If we see things as they <hi type="italic">will</hi> appear then, we shall see them as they <hi type="italic">should</hi> appear now. <div eID="gen22727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22728" type="x-p"/> The great encouragement to steadfastness in religion is taken from the second coming of Christ, considering it, <div eID="gen22728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22729" type="x-p"/> [1.] As his honour; <hi type="italic">The Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father, with his angels.</hi> To look upon Christ in his state of humiliation, so abased, so abused, <hi type="italic">a reproach of men, and despised of the people,</hi> would discourage his followers from taking any pains, or running any hazards for him; but with an eye of faith to see the Captain of our salvation coming in his glory, in all the pomp and power of the upper world, will animate us, and make us think nothing too much to do, or too hard to suffer, or him. <hi type="italic">The Son of man shall come.</hi> He here gives himself the title of his humble state (he is the <hi type="italic">Son of man</hi>), to show that he is not ashamed to own it. His first coming was in the meanness of his children, who being partakers of flesh, he took part of the same; but his second coming will be in the glory of his Father. At his first coming, he was attended with poor disciples; at his second coming, he will be attended with glorious angels; and <hi type="italic">if we suffer with him, we shall be glorified with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.12">2 Tim. ii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen22729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22730" type="x-p"/> [2.] As our concern; <hi type="italic">Then he shall reward every man according to his works.</hi> Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Jesus Christ will come as a Judge, to dispense rewards and punishments, infinitely exceeding the greatest that any earthly potentate has the dispensing of. The terror of men's tribunal (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.18">ch. x. 18</reference>) will be taken off by a believing prospect of the glory of Christ's tribunal. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Men will then be rewarded, not according to their gains in this world, but according to their works, according to what they were and did. In that day, the treachery of backsliders will be punished with eternal destruction, and the constancy of faithful souls recompensed with a crown of life. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The best preparative for that day is to <hi type="italic">deny ourselves, and take up our cross, and follow Christ;</hi> for so we shall make the Judge our Friend, and these things will then pass well in the account. <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> The rewarding of men according to their works is deferred till that day. Here good and evil seem to be dispensed promiscuously; we see not apostasy punished with immediate strokes, nor fidelity encouraged with immediate smiles, from heaven; but in that day all will be set to rights. Therefore <hi type="italic">judge nothing before the time,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.6-2Tim.4.8">2 Tim. iv. 6-8</reference>. <div eID="gen22730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22731" type="x-p"/> (2.) The near approach of his kingdom in this world, <reference osisRef="Matt.16.28">v. 28</reference>. It was so near, that there were some attending him who should live to see it. As Simeon was assured that he should not see death till he had seen the Lord's Christ come in the flesh; so some here are assured that they shall not taste death (death is a sensible thing, its terrors are seen, its bitterness is tasted) till they had seen the Lord's Christ coming in his kingdom. At the end of time, he shall come in his Father's glory; but now, in the fulness of time, he was to come in his own kingdom, his mediatorial kingdom. Some little specimen was given of his glory a few days after this, in his transfiguration (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.1">ch. xvii. 1</reference>); then he tried his robes. But this points at Christ's coming by the pouring out of his Spirit, the planting of the gospel church, the destruction of Jerusalem, and the taking away of the place and nation of the Jews, who were the most bitter enemies to Christianity. Here was <hi type="italic">the Son of man coming in his kingdom.</hi> Many then present lived to see it, particularly John, who lived till after the destruction of Jerusalem, and saw Christianity planted in the world. Let <hi type="italic">this</hi> encourage the followers of Christ to suffer for him, [1.] That their undertaking shall be succeeded; the apostles were employed in setting up Christ's kingdom; let them know, for their comfort, that whatever opposition they meet with, yet they shall carry their point, shall <hi type="italic">see of the travail of their soul.</hi> Note, It is a great encouragement to suffering saints to be assured, not only of the safety, but of the advancement of Christ's kingdom among men; not only <hi type="italic">notwithstanding</hi> their sufferings, but <hi type="italic">by</hi> their sufferings. A believing prospect of the success of the kingdom of grace, as well as of our share in the kingdom of glory, may carry us cheerfully through our sufferings. [2.] That their cause shall be pleaded; their deaths shall be revenged, and their persecutors reckoned with. [3.] That this shall be done shortly, in the present age. Note, The nearer the church's deliverances are, the more cheerful should we be in our sufferings for Christ. <hi type="italic">Behold the Judge standeth before the door.</hi> It is spoken as a favour to those that should survive the present cloudy time, that they should see better days. Note, It is desirable to share with the church in her joys, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.12">Dan. xii. 12</reference>. Observe, Christ saith, <hi type="italic">Some</hi> shall live to see those glorious days, not <hi type="italic">all;</hi> some shall enter into the promised land, but others shall fall in the wilderness. He does not tell them <hi type="italic">who</hi> shall live to see this kingdom, lest if they had known, they should have put off the thoughts of dying, but <hi type="italic">some</hi> of them shall; <hi type="italic">Behold, the Lord is at hand. The Judge standeth before the door; be patient, therefore, brethren.</hi>  <chapter eID="Matt.16"/> <div eID="gen22731" type="x-p"/>

entries.cbf38ee640fec108bfd3798221ad7a51edc14da0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13652"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.16.1-Matt.16.12">Mt 16:1-12</reference>. A Sign from Heaven Sought and Refused--Caution against the Leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees.</title> <div sID="gen26144" type="x-p"/> For the exposition, see on <reference osisRef="Mark.8.11-Mark.8.21">Mr 8:11-21</reference>.<div eID="gen26144" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.16.13-Matt.16.28">Mt 16:13-28</reference>. Peter's Noble Confession of Christ and the Benediction Pronounced upon Him--Christ's First Explicit Announcement of His Approaching Sufferings, Death, and Resurrection--His Rebuke of Peter and Warning to All the Twelve. ( = <reference osisRef="Mark.8.27">Mr 8:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.9.1">9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.18-Luke.9.27">Lu 9:18-27</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26145" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The time of this section--</hi>which is beyond doubt, and will presently be mentioned--is of immense importance, and throws a touching interest around the incidents which it records.<div eID="gen26145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26146" type="x-p"/> Peter's Confession, and the Benediction Pronounced upon Him. (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.13-Matt.16.20">Mt 16:13-20</reference>).<div eID="gen26146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26147" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13652"/><hi type="bold">13. When Jesus came into the coasts--</hi>"the parts," that is, the territory or region. In Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.27">Mr 8:27</reference>) it is "the towns" or "villages."<div eID="gen26147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26148" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Cæsarea Philippi--</hi>It lay at the foot of Mount Lebanon, near the sources of the Jordan, in the territory of Dan, and at the northeast extremity of Palestine. It was originally called Panium (from a cavern in its neighborhood dedicated to the god Pan) and Paneas. Philip, the tetrarch, the only good son of Herod the Great, in whose dominions Paneas lay, having beautified and enlarged it, changed its name to Cæsarea, in honor of the Roman emperor, and added Philippi after his own name, to distinguish it from the other Cæsarea (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.1">Ac 10:1</reference>) on the northeast coast of the Mediterranean Sea. [Josephus, Antiquities, 15.10,3; 18.2,1]. This quiet and distant retreat Jesus appears to have sought with the view of talking over with the Twelve the fruit of His past labors, and breaking to them for the first time the sad intelligence of His approaching death.<div eID="gen26148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26149" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he asked his disciples--</hi>"by the way," says Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.27">Mr 8:27</reference>), and "as He was alone praying," says Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.18">Lu 9:18</reference>).<div eID="gen26149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26150" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, Whom--</hi>or more grammatically, "Who"<div eID="gen26150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26151" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">do men say that I the Son of man am?--</hi>(or, "that the Son of man is"--the recent editors omitting here the me of Mark and Luke [Mr 8:27; Lu 9:18]; though the evidence seems pretty nearly balanced)--that is, "What are the views generally entertained of Me, the Son of man, after going up and down among them so long?" He had now closed the first great stage of His ministry, and was just entering on the last dark one. His spirit, burdened, sought relief in retirement, not only from the multitude, but even for a season from the Twelve. He retreated into "the secret place of the Most High," pouring out His soul "in supplications and prayers, with strong crying and tears" (<reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">He 5:7</reference>). On rejoining His disciples, and as they were pursuing their quiet journey, He asked them this question. <div eID="gen26151" type="x-p"/>
entries.e23b3dfab7bc62dccac7abc52b392d85c0d9140f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13653"/><div sID="gen26152" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13653"/><hi type="bold">14. And they said, Some say that thou art John the Baptist--</hi>risen from the dead. So that Herod Antipas was not singular in his surmise (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.1">Mt 14:1</reference>, 2).<div eID="gen26152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26153" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">some, Elias--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Mark.6.15">Mr 6:15</reference>).<div eID="gen26153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26154" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and others, Jeremias--</hi>Was this theory suggested by a supposed resemblance between the "Man of Sorrows" and "the weeping prophet?"<div eID="gen26154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26155" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or one of the prophets--</hi>or, as Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.8">Lu 9:8</reference>) expresses it, "that one of the old prophets is risen again." In another report of the popular opinions which Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.15">Mr 6:15</reference>) gives us, it is thus expressed, "That it is a prophet [or], as one of the prophets": in other words, That He was a prophetical person, resembling those of old. <div eID="gen26155" type="x-p"/>
entries.c2b4f5056dd412b1bc47bfde29855d482ee0d471: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13654"/><div sID="gen26156" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13654"/><hi type="bold">15. He saith unto them, But whom--</hi>rather, "who."<div eID="gen26156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26157" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">say ye that I am?--</hi>He had never put this question before, but the crisis He was reaching made it fitting that He should now have it from them. We may suppose this to be one of those moments of which the prophet says, in His name, "Then I said, I have labored in vain; I have spent my strength for naught, and in vain" (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>): Lo, these three years I come seeking fruit on this fig tree; and what is it? As the result of all, I am taken for John the Baptist, for Elias, for Jeremias, for one of the prophets. Yet some there are that have beheld My glory, the glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father, and I shall hear their voice, for it is sweet. <div eID="gen26157" type="x-p"/>
entries.755f872d4d7e6731f74d70aced6eed5d531f8d85: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13655"/><div sID="gen26158" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13655"/><hi type="bold">16. And Simon Peter answered and said, Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God--</hi>He does not say, "Scribes and Pharisees, rulers and people, are all perplexed; and shall we, unlettered fishermen, presume to decide?" But feeling the light of his Master's glory shining in his soul, he breaks forth--not in a tame, prosaic acknowledgment, "I <hi type="bold">believe that Thou art," &c.--</hi>but in the language of adoration--such as one uses in worship, "Thou Art the Christ, the Son of the Living God!" He first owns Him the promised Messiah (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.1.16">Mt 1:16</reference>); then he rises higher, echoing the voice from heaven--"This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased"; and in the important addition--"Son of the Living God"--he recognizes the essential and eternal life of God as in this His Son--though doubtless without that distinct perception afterwards vouchsafed. <div eID="gen26158" type="x-p"/>
entries.422d437209f295c2a208a4cffd3ec6a75dd95edb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13656"/><div sID="gen26159" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13656"/><hi type="bold">17. And Jesus answered and said unto him, Blessed art thou--</hi>Though it is not to be doubted that Peter, in this noble testimony to Christ, only expressed the conviction of all the Twelve, yet since he alone seems to have had clear enough apprehensions to put that conviction in proper and suitable words, and courage enough to speak them out, and readiness enough to do this at the right time--so he only, of all the Twelve, seems to have met the present want, and communicated to the saddened soul of the Redeemer at the critical moment that balm which was needed to cheer and refresh it. Nor is Jesus above giving indication of the deep satisfaction which this speech yielded Him, and hastening to respond to it by a signal acknowledgment of Peter in return.<div eID="gen26159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26160" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Simon Bar-jona--</hi>or, "son of Jona" (<reference osisRef="John.1.42">Joh 1:42</reference>), or "Jonas" (<reference osisRef="John.21.15">Joh 21:15</reference>). This name, denoting his humble fleshly extraction, seems to have been purposely here mentioned, to contrast the more vividly with the spiritual elevation to which divine illumination had raised him.<div eID="gen26160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26161" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for flesh and blood hath not revealed it unto thee--</hi>"This is not the fruit of human teaching."<div eID="gen26161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26162" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but my Father which is in heaven--</hi>In speaking of God, Jesus, it is to be observed, never calls Him, "our Father" (see on <reference osisRef="John.20.17">Joh 20:17</reference>), but either "your Father"--when He would encourage His timid believing ones with the assurance that He was theirs, and teach themselves to call Him so--or, as here, "My Father," to signify some peculiar action or aspect of Him as "the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ." <div eID="gen26162" type="x-p"/>
entries.55b9696e11fbbf9c39af1de3217a41a2cc0ba52d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13657"/><div sID="gen26163" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13657"/><hi type="bold">18. And I say also unto thee--</hi>that is, "As thou hast borne such testimony to Me, even so in return do I to thee."<div eID="gen26163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26164" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">That thou art Peter--</hi>At his first calling, this new name was announced to him as an honor afterwards to be conferred on him (<reference osisRef="John.1.43">Joh 1:43</reference>). Now he gets it, with an explanation of what it was meant to convey.<div eID="gen26164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26165" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and upon this rock--</hi>As "Peter" and "Rock" are one word in the dialect familiarly spoken by our Lord--the Aramaic or Syro-Chaldaic, which was the mother tongue of the country--this exalted play upon the word can be fully seen only in languages which have one word for both. Even in the Greek it is imperfectly represented. In French, as Webster and Wilkinson remark, it is perfect, Pierre--pierre.<div eID="gen26165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26166" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I will build my Church--</hi>not on the man Simon Bar-jona; but on him as the heavenly-taught confessor of a faith. "My Church," says our Lord, calling the Church His Own; a magnificent expression regarding Himself, remarks Bengel--nowhere else occurring in the Gospels.<div eID="gen26166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26167" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and the gates of hell--</hi>"of Hades," or, the unseen world; meaning, the gates of Death: in other words, "It shall never perish." Some explain it of "the assaults of the powers of darkness"; but though that expresses a glorious truth, probably the former is the sense here. <div eID="gen26167" type="x-p"/>
entries.a850ffce9014551eda3ca546449168aae30e541d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13658"/><div sID="gen26168" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13658"/><hi type="bold">19. And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven--</hi>the kingdom of God about to be set up on earth<div eID="gen26168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26169" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven--</hi>Whatever this mean, it was soon expressly extended to all the apostles (<reference osisRef="Matt.18.18">Mt 18:18</reference>); so that the claim of supreme authority in the Church, made for Peter by the Church of Rome, and then arrogated to themselves by the popes as the legitimate successors of St. Peter, is baseless and impudent. As first in confessing Christ, Peter got this commission before the rest; and with these "keys," on the day of Pentecost, he first "opened the door of faith" to the Jews, and then, in the person of Cornelius, he was honored to do the same to the Gentiles. Hence, in the lists of the apostles, Peter is always first named. See on <reference osisRef="Matt.18.18">Mt 18:18</reference>. One thing is clear, that not in all the New Testament is there the vestige of any authority either claimed or exercised by Peter, or conceded to him, above the rest of the apostles--a thing conclusive against the Romish claims in behalf of that apostle. <div eID="gen26169" type="x-p"/>
entries.1e7d5c7c58133b924bcd2b481b232405e06d6fb1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13659"/><div sID="gen26170" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13659"/><hi type="bold">20. Then charged he his disciples that they should tell no man that he was Jesus the Christ--</hi>Now that He had been so explicit, they might naturally think the time come for giving it out openly; but here they are told it had not.<div eID="gen26170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26171" type="x-p"/> Announcement of His Approaching Death and Rebuke of Peter (<reference osisRef="Matt.16.21-Matt.16.28">Mt 16:21-28</reference>).<div eID="gen26171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26172" type="x-p"/> The occasion here is evidently the same. <div eID="gen26172" type="x-p"/>
entries.5be5b52caecf55c78195b9e81721046bc721b21a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13660"/><div sID="gen26173" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13660"/><hi type="bold">21. From that time forth began Jesus to show unto his disciples--</hi>that is, with an explicitness and frequency He had never observed before.<div eID="gen26173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26174" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">how that he must go unto Jerusalem and suffer many things--</hi>"and be rejected," (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.31">Mr 8:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.22">Lu 9:22</reference>).<div eID="gen26174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26175" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the elders and chief priests and scribes--</hi>not as before, merely by not receiving Him, but by formal deeds.<div eID="gen26175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26176" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and be killed, and be raised again the third day--</hi>Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.32">Mr 8:32</reference>) adds, that "He spake that saying openly"--"explicitly," or "without disguise." <div eID="gen26176" type="x-p"/>
entries.5adb00dca63e32a1e32be7e2d191d6f17e320c90: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13661"/><div sID="gen26177" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13661"/><hi type="bold">22. Then Peter took him--</hi>aside, apart from the rest; presuming on the distinction just conferred on him; showing how unexpected and distasteful to them all was the announcement.<div eID="gen26177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26178" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and began to rebuke him--</hi>affectionately, yet with a certain generous indignation, to chide Him.<div eID="gen26178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26179" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">saying, Be it far from thee: this shall not be unto thee--</hi>that is, "If I can help it": the same spirit that prompted him in the garden to draw the sword in His behalf (<reference osisRef="John.18.10">Joh 18:10</reference>). <div eID="gen26179" type="x-p"/>
entries.f659969164e1e532ae644c747b5f91245c4b60ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13662"/><div sID="gen26180" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13662"/><hi type="bold">23. But he turned, and said--</hi>in the hearing of the rest; for Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.33">Mr 8:33</reference>) expressly says, "When He had turned about and looked on His disciples, He rebuked Peter"; perceiving that he had but boldly uttered what others felt, and that the check was needed by them also.<div eID="gen26180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26181" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Get thee behind me, Satan--</hi>the same words as He had addressed to the Tempter (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.8">Lu 4:8</reference>); for He felt in it a satanic lure, a whisper from hell, to move Him from His purpose to suffer. So He shook off the Serpent, then coiling around Him, and "felt no harm" (<reference osisRef="Acts.28.5">Ac 28:5</reference>). How quickly has the "rock" turned to a devil! The fruit of divine teaching the Lord delighted to honor in Peter; but the mouthpiece of hell, which he had in a moment of forgetfulness become, the Lord shook off with horror.<div eID="gen26181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26182" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou art an offence--</hi>a stumbling-block.<div eID="gen26182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26183" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto me--</hi>"Thou playest the Tempter, casting a stumbling-block in My way to the Cross. Could it succeed, where wert thou? and how should the Serpent's head be bruised?"<div eID="gen26183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26184" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for thou savourest not--</hi>thou thinkest not.<div eID="gen26184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26185" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the things that be of God, but those that be of men--</hi>"Thou art carried away by human views of the way of setting up Messiah's kingdom, quite contrary to those of God." This was kindly said, not to take off the sharp edge of the rebuke, but to explain and justify it, as it was evident Peter knew not what was in the bosom of his rash speech. <div eID="gen26185" type="x-p"/>
entries.f9507f735fa38268476721dab6ec561ba1fbf3fa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13663"/><div sID="gen26186" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13663"/><hi type="bold">24. Then said Jesus unto his disciples--</hi>Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.34">Mr 8:34</reference>) says, "When He had called the people unto Him, with His disciples also, He said unto them"--turning the rebuke of one into a warning to all.<div eID="gen26186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26187" type="x-p"/> If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me. <div eID="gen26187" type="x-p"/>
entries.18bc344b0719e658970e4b74b29819577878b850: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13664"/><div sID="gen26188" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13664"/><hi type="bold">25. For whosoever will save--</hi>is minded to save, or bent on saving.<div eID="gen26188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26189" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his life shall lose it, and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.10.38">Mt 10:38</reference>,<reference osisRef="Matt.10.39">39</reference>). "A suffering and dying Messiah liketh you ill; but what if His servants shall meet the same fate? They may not; but who follows Me must be prepared for the worst." <div eID="gen26189" type="x-p"/>
entries.16ea67b0c1d4227409b26c37dc734c3fdc5d940b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13665"/><div sID="gen26190" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13665"/><hi type="bold">26. For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul--</hi>or forfeit his own soul?<div eID="gen26190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26191" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?--</hi>Instead of these weighty words, which we find in <reference osisRef="Mark.8.36">Mr 8:36</reference> also, it is thus expressed in <reference osisRef="Luke.9.25">Lu 9:25</reference>: "If he gain the whole world, and lose himself, or be cast away," or better, "If he gain the whole world, and destroy or forfeit himself." How awful is the stake as here set forth! If a man makes the present world--in its various forms of riches, honors, pleasures, and such like--the object of supreme pursuit, be it that he gains the world; yet along with it he forfeits his own soul. Not that any ever did, or ever will gain the whole world--a very small portion of it, indeed, falls to the lot of the most successful of the world's votaries--but to make the extravagant concession, that by giving himself entirely up to it, a man gains the whole world; yet, setting over against this gain the forfeiture of his soul--necessarily following the surrender of his whole heart to the world--what is he profited? But, if not the whole world, yet possibly something else may be conceived as an equivalent for the soul. Well, what is it?--"Or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?" Thus, in language the weightiest, because the simplest, does our Lord shut up His hearers, and all who shall read these words to the end of the world, to the priceless value to every man of his own soul. In Mark and Luke (<reference osisRef="Mark.8.38">Mr 8:38</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.26">Lu 9:26</reference>) the following words are added: "Whosoever therefore shall be ashamed of Me and of My words [shall be ashamed of belonging to Me, and ashamed of My Gospel] in this adulterous and sinful generation" (see on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.39">Mt 12:39</reference>), "of him shall the Son of man be ashamed when He cometh in the glory of His Father, with the holy angels." He will render back to that man his own treatment, disowning him before the most august of all assemblies, and putting him to "shame and everlasting contempt" (<reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Da 12:2</reference>). "O shame," exclaims Bengel, "to be put to shame before God, Christ, and angels!" The sense of shame is founded on our love of reputation, which causes instinctive aversion to what is fitted to lower it, and was given us as a preservative from all that is properly shameful. To be lost to shame is to be nearly past hope. (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.5">Zep 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.15">Jr 6:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">3:3</reference>). But when Christ and "His words" are unpopular, the same instinctive desire to stand well with others begets that temptation to be ashamed of Him which only the expulsive power of a higher affection can effectually counteract. <div eID="gen26191" type="x-p"/>
entries.a4096a264fa0c7c848b002ba9addd4207f8562ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13666"/><div sID="gen26192" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13666"/><hi type="bold">27. For the Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels--</hi>in the splendor of His Father's authority and with all His angelic ministers, ready to execute His pleasure.<div eID="gen26192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26193" type="x-p"/> and then he shall reward, &c. <div eID="gen26193" type="x-p"/>
entries.c13b41c04aad066d4e6027e2d58500fe35cbc6eb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13667"/><div sID="gen26194" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13667"/><hi type="bold">28. Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here--</hi>"some of those standing here."<div eID="gen26194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26195" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which shall not taste of death, fill they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom--</hi>or, as in Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.9.1">Mr 9:1</reference>), "till they see the kingdom of God come with power"; or, as in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.27">Lu 9:27</reference>), more simply still, "till they see the kingdom of God." The reference, beyond doubt, is to the firm establishment and victorious progress, in the lifetime of some then present, of that new kingdom of Christ, which was destined to work the greatest of all changes on this earth, and be the grand pledge of His final coming in glory. <chapter eID="Matt.16"/>

entries.e53b0f38a4a51003a141daca4e2fe8c7fb45d8d8: <div eID="gen37613" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen37614" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37615" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37615" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen37614" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen37616" type="x-p"/> The Pharisees insidiously require our Lord to give them a sign, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.1">Mat 16:1</reference>. They are severely rebuked for their hypocrisy and wickedness, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.2-Mat.16.5">Mat 16:2-5</reference>. The disciples are cautioned to beware of them and their destructive doctrine, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.6-Mat.16.12">Mat 16:6-12</reference>. The different opinions formed by the people of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.13">Mat 16:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.14">Mat 16:14</reference>. Peter's confession, and our Lord's discourse on it, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.15-Mat.16.20">Mat 16:15-20</reference>. He foretells his sufferings, and reproves Peter, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.21-Mat.16.23">Mat 16:21-23</reference>. Teaches the necessity of self-denial, and shows the reasons on which it is founded, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.24-Mat.16.26">Mat 16:24-26</reference>. Speaks of a future judgment, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.27">Mat 16:27</reference>. And promises the speedy opening of the glory of his own kingdom on earth, <reference osisRef="Mat.16.28">Mat 16:28</reference>. <div eID="gen37616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37617" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen37617" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37618" type="x-p"/> The Pharisees also with the Sadducees - Though a short account of these has been already given in a note on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.7">Mat 3:7</reference>, yet, as one more detailed may be judged necessary, I think it proper to introduce it in this place. <div eID="gen37618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37619" type="x-p"/> The Pharisees were the most considerable sect among the Jews, for they had not only the scribes, and all the learned men of the law of their party, but they also drew after them the bulk of the people. When this sect arose is uncertain. Josephus, Antiq. lib. v. c. xiii. s. 9, speaks of them as existing about 144 years before the Christian era. They had their appellation of Pharisees, from פרש parash, to separate, and were probably, in their rise, the most holy people among the Jews, having separated themselves from the national corruption, with a design to restore and practice the pure worship of the most High. That they were greatly degenerated in our Lord's time is sufficiently evident; but still we may learn, from their external purity and exactness, that their principles in the beginning were holy. Our Lord testifies that they had cleansed the outside of the cup and the platter, but within they were full of abomination. They still kept up the outward regulations of the institution, but they had utterly lost its spirit; and hypocrisy was the only substitute now in their power for that spirit of piety which I suppose, and not unreasonably, characterized the origin of this sect. <div eID="gen37619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37620" type="x-p"/> As to their religious opinions, they still continued to credit the being of a God; they received the five books of Moses, the writings of the prophets, and the hagiographa. The hagiographa or holy writings, from αγιος holy, and γραφω I write, included the twelve following books - Psalms, Proverbs, Job, Canticles, Ruth, Lamentations, Ecclesiastes, Esther, Daniel, Ezra, Nehemiah, and Chronicles. These, among the Jews, occupied a middle place between the law and the prophets, as divinely inspired. The Pharisees believed, in a confused way, in the resurrection, though they received the Pythagorean doctrine of the metempsychosis, or transmigration of souls. Those, however, who were notoriously wicked, they consigned, on their death, immediately to hell, without the benefit of transmigration, or the hope of future redemption. They held also the predestinarian doctrine of necessity, and the government of the world by fate; and yet, inconsistently, allowed some degree of liberty to the human will. See Prideaux. <div eID="gen37620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37621" type="x-p"/> The Sadducees had their origin and name from one Sadoc, a disciple of Antigonus of Socho, president of the Sanhedrin, and teacher of the law in one of the great divinity schools in Jerusalem, about 264 years before the incarnation. <div eID="gen37621" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37622" type="x-p"/> This Antigonus having often in his lectures informed his scholars, that they should not serve God through expectation of a reward, but through love and filial reverence only, Sadoc inferred from this teaching that there were neither rewards nor punishments after this life, and, by consequence, that there was no resurrection of the dead, nor angel, nor spirit, in the invisible world; and that man is to be rewarded or punished here for the good or evil he does. <div eID="gen37622" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37623" type="x-p"/> They received only the five books of Moses, and rejected all unwritten traditions. From every account we have of this sect, it plainly appears they were a kind of mongrel deists, and professed materialists. See Prideaux, and the authors he quotes, Connex. vol. iii. p. 95, and 471, etc., and see the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.7">Mat 3:7</reference>. <div eID="gen37623" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37624" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Mat.22.16">Mat 22:16</reference>, we shall meet with a third sect, called Herodians, of whom a few words may be spoken here, It is allowed on all hands that these did not exist before the time of Herod the Great, who died only three years after the incarnation of our Lord. What the opinions of these were is not agreed among the learned. Many of the primitive fathers believed that their distinguishing doctrine was, that they held Herod to be the Messiah; but it is not likely that such an opinion could prevail in our Savior's time, thirty years after Herod's death, when not one characteristic of Messiahship had appeared in him during his life. Others suppose that they were Herod's courtiers, who flattered the passions of their master, and, being endowed with a convenient conscience, changed with the times; but, as Herod was now dead upwards of thirty years, such a sect could not exist in reference to him; and yet all allow that they derived their origin from Herod the Great. <div eID="gen37624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37625" type="x-p"/> Our Lord says, <reference osisRef="Mar.8.15">Mar 8:15</reference>, that they had the leaven of Herod, i.e. a bad doctrine, which they received from him. What this was may be easily discovered: <div eID="gen37625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37626" type="x-p"/> 1. Herod subjected himself and his people to the dominion of the Romans, in opposition to that law, <reference osisRef="Deu.17.15">Deu 17:15</reference>, Thou shalt not set a king over thee - which is not thy brother, i.e. one out of the twelve tribes. <div eID="gen37626" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37627" type="x-p"/> 2. He built temples, sat up images, and joined in heathenish worship, though he professed the Jewish religion; and this was in opposition to all the law and the prophets. <div eID="gen37627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37628" type="x-p"/> From this we may learn that the Herodians were such as, first, held it lawful to transfer the Divine government to a heathen ruler; and, secondly, to conform occasionally to heathenish rites in their religious worship. In short, they appear to have been persons who trimmed between God and the world - who endeavored to reconcile his service with that of mammon - and who were religious just as far as it tended to secure their secular interests. It is probable that this sect was at last so blended with, that it became lost in, the sect of the Sadducees; for the persons who art called Herodians, <reference osisRef="Mar.8.15">Mar 8:15</reference>, are styled Sadducees in <reference osisRef="Mat.16.6">Mat 16:6</reference>. See Prideaux, Con. vol. iii. p. 516, etc., and Josephus, Antiq. b. xv. c. viii. s. i. and x. s. iii. But it is very likely that the Herodians, mentioned c. xxii. 10, were courtiers or servants of Herod king of Galilee. See the note there. <div eID="gen37628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37629" type="x-p"/> Show them a sign - These sects, however opposed among themselves, most cordially unite in their opposition to Christ and his truth. That the kingdom of Satan may not fall, all his subjects must fight against the doctrine and maxims of the kingdom of Christ. <div eID="gen37629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37630" type="x-p"/> Tempting - him - Feigning a desire to have his doctrine fully proved to them, that they might credit it, and become his disciples; but having no other design than to betray and ruin him.
entries.0ad343c94ebda9eff6e7af50bfc7e2cf3e48ba4a: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen37630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37631" type="x-p"/> When it is evening - There are certain signs of fair and foul weather, which ye are in the constant habit of observing, and which do not fail. - The signs of the times: the doctrine which I preach, and the miracles which I work among you, are as sure signs that the day-spring from on high has visited you for your salvation; but if ye refute to hear, and continue in darkness, the red and gloomy cloud of vindictive justice shall pour out such a storm of wrath upon you as shalt sweep you from the face of the earth.
entries.f791d306e4ff6f16d3a5151b224223f9871d9a59: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen37631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37632" type="x-p"/> The sky is red and lowering - The signs of fair and foul weather were observed in a similar manner among the Romans, and indeed among most other people. Many treatises have been written on the subject: thus a poet: - <div eID="gen37632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37633" type="x-p"/> Caeruleus pluviam denunciant, Igneus euros <div eID="gen37633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37634" type="x-p"/> Sin Maculae incipient Rutilo immiscerier Igni, <div eID="gen37634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37635" type="x-p"/> Omnia tunc pariter Vento Nimbisque videbis <div eID="gen37635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37636" type="x-p"/> Fervere Virg. Geor. i. l. 453 "If fiery red his glowing globe descends, <div eID="gen37636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37637" type="x-p"/> High winds and furious tempests he portends: <div eID="gen37637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37638" type="x-p"/> But if his cheeks are swoll'n with livid blue, <div eID="gen37638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37639" type="x-p"/> He bodes wet weather, by his watery hue <div eID="gen37639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37640" type="x-p"/> If dusky spots are varied on his brow, <div eID="gen37640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37641" type="x-p"/> And streak'd with red a troubled color show, <div eID="gen37641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37642" type="x-p"/> That sullen mixture shall at once declare, <div eID="gen37642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37643" type="x-p"/> Wind, rain, and storms, and elemental war <div eID="gen37643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37644" type="x-p"/> Dryden.
entries.0744a6cc94c3eaec67382a6b7c6203fbb4c6ff80: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen37644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37645" type="x-p"/> Wicked and adulterous generation - The Jewish people are represented in the Sacred Writings as married to the Most High; but, like a disloyal wife, forsaking their true husband, and uniting themselves to Satan and sin. Seeketh after a sign, σημειον επιζητει, seeketh sign upon sign, or, still another sign. Our blessed Lord had already wrought miracles sufficient to demonstrate both his Divine mission and his divinity; only one was farther necessary to take away the scandal of his cross and death, to fulfill the Scriptures, and to establish the Christian religion; and that was, his resurrection from the dead, which, he here states, was typified in the case of Jonah.
entries.1ccb2adce4ed2a33ff7f5406a9602df007e19527: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen37645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37646" type="x-p"/> Come to the other side - Viz. the coast of Bethsaida, by which our Lord passed, going to Caesarea, for he was now on his journey thither. See <reference osisRef="Mat.16.13">Mat 16:13</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Mar.8.22">Mar 8:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.8.27">Mar 8:27</reference>.
entries.7dcae86e765f5d0bff3598e1e1c58720ce41ceed: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen37646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37647" type="x-p"/> Beware of the leaven - What the leaven of Pharisees and Sadducees was has been already explained, see <reference osisRef="Mat.16.1">Mat 16:1</reference>. Bad doctrines act in the soul as leaven does in meal; they assimulate the whole Spirit to their own nature. A man's particular creed has a greater influence on his tempers and conduct than most are aware of. Pride, hypocrisy, and worldly-mindedness, which constituted the leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees, ruin the major part of the world.
entries.0a38bdde56d22109692af60d218f81edd735ba11: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen37647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37648" type="x-p"/> They reasoned - For, as Lightfoot observes, the term leaven was very rarely used among the Jews to signify doctrine, and therefore the disciples did not immediately apprehend his meaning. In what a lamentable state of blindness is the human mind? Bodily wants are perceived with the utmost readiness, and a supply is sought with all speed. But the necessities of the soul are rarely discovered, though they are more pressing than those of the body, and the supply of them of infinitely more importance.
entries.4653e95ff1479d11fb864238e4345d3615d55bc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen37648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37649" type="x-p"/> When Jesus perceived, he said - Αυτοις, unto them, is wanting in BDKLMS, and twenty others; one of the Syriac, the Armenian, Ethiopia, Vulgate, and most of the Itala; also in Origen, Theophylact, and Lucifer Calaritanus. Mill approves of the omission, and Griesbach has left it out of the text. <div eID="gen37649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37650" type="x-p"/> O ye of little faith - There are degrees in faith, as well as in the other graces of the Spirit. Little faith may be the seed of great faith, and therefore is not to be despised. But many who should be strong in faith have but a small measure of it, because they either give way to sin, or are not careful to improve what God has already given.
entries.f57a3c46a8a810de25c3de4b9fa2d5ced7027676: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen37650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37651" type="x-p"/> Do ye not yet understand - the five loaves - neither the seven - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.14.14">Mat 14:14</reference>, etc. How astonishing is it that these men should have any fear of lacking bread, after having seen the two miracles which our blessed Lord alludes to above! Though men quickly perceive their bodily wants, and are querulous enough till they get them supplied, yet they as quickly forget the mercy which they had received; and thus God gets few returns of gratitude for his kindnesses. To make men, therefore, deeply sensible of his favors, he is induced to suffer them often to be in want, and then to supply them in such a way as to prove that their supply has come immediately from the hand of their bountiful Father.
entries.37c5150b0366e259185f0eac77a62d5f6c23c3ce: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen37651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37652" type="x-p"/> How is it that ye do not understand - We are not deficient in spiritual knowledge, because we have not had sufficient opportunities of acquainting ourselves with God; but because we did not improve the advantages we had. How deep and ruinous must our ignorance be, if God did not give line upon line, precept upon precept, here a little and there a little! They now perceived that he warned them against the superstition of the Pharisees, which produced hypocrisy, pride, envy, etc., and the false doctrine of the Sadducees, which denied the existence of a spiritual world, the immortality of the soul, the resurrection of the body, and the providence of God.
entries.c2c0d3f0adefdf40ba2139487540a7d21762b418: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen37652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37653" type="x-p"/> Caesarea Philippi - A city, in the tribe of Naphtali, near to Mount Libanus, in the province of Iturea. Its ancient name was Dan, <reference osisRef="Gen.14.14">Gen 14:14</reference>; afterwards it was called Lais, <reference osisRef="Jdg.18.7">Jdg 18:7</reference>. But Philip the tetrarch, having rebuilt and beautified it, gave it the name of Caesarea, in honor of Tiberius Caesar, the reigning emperor: but to distinguish it from another Caesarea, which was on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, and to perpetuate the fame of him who rebuilt it, it was called Caesarea Philippi, or Caesarea of Philip. <div eID="gen37653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37654" type="x-p"/> When Jesus came - Ελθων δε ο Ιησους - when Jesus was coming. Not, when Jesus came, or was come, for Mark expressly mentions that it happened εν τη οδω, in the way to Caesarea Philippi, <reference osisRef="Mar.8.27">Mar 8:27</reference>, and he is Matthew's best interpreter. - Wakefield. <div eID="gen37654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37655" type="x-p"/> Whom do men say - He asked his disciples this question, not because he was ignorant what the people thought and spoke of him; but to have the opportunity, in getting an express declaration of their faith from themselves, to confirm and strengthen them in it: but see on <reference osisRef="Luk.9.20">Luk 9:20</reference> (note). Some, John the Baptist, etc. By this and other passages we learn, that the Pharisaic doctrine of the Metempsychosis, or transmigration of souls, was pretty general; for it was upon this ground that they believed that the soul of the Baptist, or of Elijah, Jeremiah, or some of the prophets, had come to a new life in the body of Jesus.
entries.bcf9332f202951aeada3d88a96cb27733c0c1a66: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen37655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37656" type="x-p"/> Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God - Every word here is emphatic - a most concise, and yet comprehensive, confession of faith. <div eID="gen37656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37657" type="x-p"/> The Christ, or Messiah, points out his divinity, and shows his office; the Son - designates his person: on this account it is that both are joined together so frequently in the new covenant. Of the living God Του Θεου, του ζωντος, literally, of God the Living One. The C. Bezae has for Του ζωντος the Living One, Του σωζοντος, the Savior, and the Cant. Dei Salvatoris, of God the Savior. <div eID="gen37657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37658" type="x-p"/> Living - a character applied to the Supreme Being, not only to distinguish him from the dead idols of paganism, but also to point him out as the source of life, present, spiritual, and eternal. Probably there is an allusion here to the great name יהוה Yeve, or Yehovah, which properly signifies being or existence.
entries.8886df5ca05f3d7da46b2667439f4010d345e902: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen37658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37659" type="x-p"/> Blessed art thou, Simon Bar-jona - Or Simon, son of Jonah; so Bar-jonah should be translated, and so it is rendered by our Lord, <reference osisRef="Joh.1.42">Joh 1:42</reference>. Flesh and blood - i.e. Man; - no human being hath revealed this; and though the text is literal enough, yet every body should know that this is a Hebrew periphrasis for man; and the literal translation of it here, and in <reference osisRef="Gal.1.16">Gal 1:16</reference>, has misled thousands, who suppose that flesh and blood signify carnal reason, as it is termed, or the unregenerate principle in man. Is it not evident, from our Lord's observation, that it requires an express revelation of God in a man's soul, to give him a saving acquaintance with Jesus Christ; and that not even the miracles of our Lord, wrought before the eyes, will effect this? The darkness must be removed from the heart by the Holy Spirit, before a man can become wise unto salvation.
entries.7d00742c2ee7777fd4649595bac53d75cbce9488: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen37659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37660" type="x-p"/> Thou art Peter - This was the same as if he had said, I acknowledge thee for one of my disciples - for this name was given him by our Lord when he first called him to the apostleship. See <reference osisRef="Joh.1.42">Joh 1:42</reference>. <div eID="gen37660" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37661" type="x-p"/> Peter, πετρος, signifies a stone, or fragment of a rock; and our Lord, whose constant custom it was to rise to heavenly things through the medium of earthly, takes occasion from the name, the metaphorical meaning of which was strength and stability, to point out the solidity of the confession, and the stability of that cause which should be founded on The Christ, the Son of the Living God. See the notes at <reference osisRef="Luk.9.62">Luk 9:62</reference>. <div eID="gen37661" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37662" type="x-p"/> Upon this very rock, επι ταυτη τη πετρα - this true confession of thine - that I am The Messiah, that am come to reveal and communicate The Living God, that the dead, lost world may be saved - upon this very rock, myself, thus confessed (alluding probably to <reference osisRef="Psa.118.22">Psa 118:22</reference>, The Stone which the builders rejected is become the Head-Stone of the Corner: and to <reference osisRef="Isa.28.16">Isa 28:16</reference>, Behold I lay a Stone in Zion for a Foundation) - will I build my Church, μου την εκκλησιαν, my assembly, or congregation, i.e. of persons who are made partakers of this precious faith. That Peter is not designed in our Lord's words must be evident to all who are not blinded by prejudice. Peter was only one of the builders in this sacred edifice, <reference osisRef="Eph.2.20">Eph 2:20</reference> who himself tells us, (with the rest of the believers), was built on this living foundation stone: <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.4">1Pet 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1Pet 2:5</reference>, therefore Jesus Christ did not say, on thee, Peter, will I build my Church, but changes immediately the expression, and says, upon that very rock, επι ταυτη τη πετρα, to show that he neither addressed Peter, nor any other of the apostles. So, the supremacy of Peter, and the infallibility of the Church of Rome, must be sought in some other scripture, for they certainly are not to be found in this. On the meaning of the word Church, see at the conclusion of this chapter. <div eID="gen37662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37663" type="x-p"/> The gates of hell, πυλαι Αδου i. e, the machinations and powers of the invisible world. In ancient times the gates of fortified cities were used to hold councils in, and were usually places of great strength. Our Lord's expression means, that neither the plots, stratagems, nor strength of Satan and his angels, should ever so far prevail as to destroy the sacred truths in the above confession. Sometimes the gates are taken for the troops which issue out from them: we may firmly believe, that though hell should open her gates, and vomit out her devil and all his angels, to fight against Christ and his saints, ruin and discomfiture must be the consequence on their part; as the arm of the Omnipotent must prevail.
entries.54500a122a64cba2ed3a2764c657fc40f3b2966f: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen37663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37664" type="x-p"/> The keys of the kingdom - By the kingdom of heaven, we may consider the true Church, that house of God, to be meant; and by the keys, the power of admitting into that house, or of preventing any improper person from coming in. In other words, the doctrine of salvation, and the full declaration of the way in which God will save sinners; and who they are that shall be finally excluded from heaven; and on what account. When the Jews made a man a doctor of the law, they put into his hand the key of the closet in the temple where the sacred books were kept, and also tablets to write upon; signifying, by this, that they gave him authority to teach, and to explain the Scriptures to the people. - Martin.
